record.subtitle: How a single uncommitted write can corrupt downstream reads, cause phantom transactions, and what isolation levels prevent it
record.summary: A dirty read occurs when Transaction B reads data written by Transaction A before A has committed. If A rolls back, B has made decisions on data that never officially existed. Trace the anomaly from storage-engine visibility rules through multi-service fan-out and the isolation settings that close it.

useCase.goal: Prevent balance, inventory, and audit decisions from acting on uncommitted writes that may still roll back.
actorsAndComponents: Primary SQL database (buffer pool / MVCC versions)
Audit log and optional cache tier
requirements: Readers of financial or inventory state must observe only committed row versions.
Rollback of an in-flight writer must not leave downstream decisions, caches, or audit records based on provisional values.
Approximate analytics may use weaker isolation only when the consumer contract is explicitly approximate.
constraints: High-concurrency OLTP with overlapping transfers and stock reservations.
Mixed engines across services; MySQL and SQL Server can still expose READ UNCOMMITTED / NOLOCK paths.
assumptions: PostgreSQL and Oracle exclude uncommitted versions from snapshots by design.
Application side effects outside the database transaction are not automatically undone by ROLLBACK.

record.markdownContent:
## A balance check that reads an unfinished transfer

It is 14:03 UTC on a payment platform. The transfer service opens a transaction, debits `acc-9981` from USD 300 to USD 60, and has not committed yet. A few milliseconds later the balance service asks whether that same account can fund another withdrawal. Under `READ UNCOMMITTED`, the balance service sees USD 60, declines a valid request, and writes a false “insufficient funds” audit record. The transfer then rolls back because a downstream bank API timed out. The account still holds USD 300. The declined request was correct. The audit log is not.

That is a dirty read: Transaction B observed a write that Transaction A never made permanent. The damage is rarely the row itself. It is the application decision, cache entry, or event that escapes before the writer aborts.

This scenario follows one uncommitted debit through storage-engine visibility rules, isolation levels, multi-service fan-out, and the configuration choices that either stop the anomaly or invite it.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    title Dirty read during an uncommitted debit
    participant T1 as Transfer service (T1)
    participant DB as Database engine
    participant T2 as Balance service (T2)
    T1->>DB: BEGIN; UPDATE accounts SET balance = 60
    Note over DB: New value is in the write buffer / new row version
    T2->>DB: SELECT balance WHERE id = 9981
    DB-->>T2: 60 (dirty, if READ UNCOMMITTED)
    Note over T2: Declines withdrawal and writes audit
    T1->>DB: ROLLBACK
    Note over DB: Balance restored to 300
    Note over T2: Decision already committed outside the row
```

## Stage 1 — Name the uncertainty window

Committed data is durable and visible to later transactions. Uncommitted data is provisional: it may exist in a buffer, undo chain, or new MVCC version, and the writer can still erase it with `ROLLBACK`. A dirty read is a read of that provisional middle state.

Two engine families expose the window differently:

- Lock-based engines prevent dirty reads when readers take shared locks that conflict with the writer’s exclusive lock. `READ UNCOMMITTED` skips that shared lock and lets the reader touch the buffered page.
- MVCC engines tag each new row version with the writing transaction id. A reader’s snapshot includes only committed creators, so an in-flight version is invisible and the previous committed version is returned instead.

``
    [*] --> Uncommitted: Writer mutates the row
    Uncommitted --> Committed: COMMIT
    Uncommitted --> RolledBack: ROLLBACK
    Committed --> [*]: Permanent for later readers
    RolledBack --> [*]: Prior committed value restored
```

The mental model is not “the database stored a wrong number.” It is “another transaction acted on a future that was cancelled.”

## Stage 2 — Watch the race at the buffer

The dirty-read timeline has four beats: T1 writes without committing, T2 reads the provisional value, T1 rolls back, and T2 keeps the decision it already made. From the engine’s point of view T2’s later `COMMIT` can still be valid. The bug lives in application logic that treated an uncommitted observation as durable truth.

```sql
-- T1 (transfer)
BEGIN;
UPDATE accounts SET balance = 60 WHERE id = 9981;
-- still open...

-- T2 (balance check) at READ UNCOMMITTED
BEGIN;
SELECT balance FROM accounts WHERE id = 9981; -- may return 60
-- declines a second withdrawal based on that value
COMMIT;

-- T1
ROLLBACK; -- balance returns to 300; T2's decision remains
```

On a locking engine at `READ UNCOMMITTED`, T2 never waits for T1’s exclusive lock. On PostgreSQL, even an attempted `READ UNCOMMITTED` session is upgraded to `READ COMMITTED`, so T2 would still see the last committed balance of 300. Engine architecture decides whether the anomaly is possible at all.

## Stage 3 — Follow the leak across services

Inside one database connection the harm is already real. Across microservices it becomes a data-contract violation that outruns the rollback.

A warehouse reservation writes stock to zero and stays uncommitted. An inventory service reads that zero under a weak isolation setting and tells the order service the SKU is unavailable. Shipping and notification pipelines act on that answer. When the warehouse rolls back, stock is 1 again, but the customer already received a cancellation and the audit trail contains a phantom stock-out.

``
    A[Warehouse service] -->|BEGIN reserve SKU-4421| B[Uncommitted write buffer]
    B -->|Weak isolation read| C[Inventory service]
    C -->|Reports zero available| D[Order service]
    D -->|Queues cancellation| E[Shipping / notify]
    A -->|ROLLBACK| F[Stock restored to 1]
    F -.->|Too late| E
```

Caches make the window longer. A Redis or Memcached entry populated from a dirty read can serve the phantom value long after the source transaction disappeared. Treat “committed read → then cache” as part of the contract for financial and inventory paths.

## Stage 4 — Choose the isolation floor that closes dirty reads

SQL isolation levels are defined by the anomalies they allow. Dirty reads are permitted only at `READ UNCOMMITTED`. `READ COMMITTED` is the first level that forbids them, and it is the default on PostgreSQL, Oracle, and SQL Server.

| Isolation level | Dirty read | Non-repeatable read | Phantom read | Write skew |
| --- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| Read Uncommitted | Possible | Possible | Possible | Possible |
| Read Committed | Prevented | Possible | Possible | Possible |
| Repeatable Read | Prevented | Prevented | Possible* | Possible* |
| Serializable | Prevented | Prevented | Prevented | Prevented |

\*InnoDB Repeatable Read also blocks many phantoms with gap locks; the SQL standard still allows phantoms at that level.

Serializable removes more anomaly classes, but under contention it increases aborts and retries. For most OLTP work, Read Committed is the correct floor for dirty-read protection. Raise isolation when the workload also needs stable multi-statement snapshots or serializable conflict detection.

## Stage 5 — Respect what each engine can actually do

The SQL standard allows dirty reads at `READ UNCOMMITTED`. Implementations diverge:

| Database | Default isolation | Can emit dirty reads? |
| --- | --- | :---: |
| PostgreSQL | Read Committed | No — MVCC excludes uncommitted versions; `READ UNCOMMITTED` is upgraded |
| MySQL InnoDB | Repeatable Read | Yes — only at `READ UNCOMMITTED` |
| Oracle | Read Committed | No — that is the minimum level |
| SQL Server | Read Committed | Yes — via `READ UNCOMMITTED` or `NOLOCK` |

PostgreSQL and Oracle are architecturally closed to dirty reads. MySQL and SQL Server are not, and SQL Server’s `WITH (NOLOCK)` is the most common accidental opt-in: developers add it for “faster reads” and silently accept dirty, non-repeatable, and phantom reads together.

```ini
# postgresql.conf — safe default already prevents dirty reads
default_transaction_isolation = 'read committed'
```

```ini
# my.cnf — keep InnoDB at least at READ-COMMITTED for OLTP
[mysqld]
transaction_isolation = READ-COMMITTED
```

```sql
-- SQL Server: prefer RCSI over NOLOCK for non-blocking committed reads
ALTER DATABASE YourDatabase SET READ_COMMITTED_SNAPSHOT ON;
```

## Stage 6 — Use weak reads only where approximation is the product

Dirty reads are sometimes an accepted trade-off when the consumer already labels the number as approximate: live “users online” counters, coarse monitoring scans, or batch reports that must not contend with OLTP writers. In those cases document the isolation choice on the endpoint or query, and never feed the result into payments, inventory commitments, compliance ledgers, or shared caches that other services treat as authoritative.

Defenses, cheapest first:

1. Audit for explicit `READ UNCOMMITTED`, `NOLOCK`, and ORM isolation overrides; remove unjustified ones.
2. Pin Read Committed (or higher) at the pool / data-source layer on MySQL and SQL Server.
3. Use Repeatable Read / Serializable snapshots for long reporting queries on MVCC engines instead of weakening isolation.
4. Add optimistic version checks when you cannot raise isolation but must detect lost updates.
5. Prefer append-only ledgers for balances that must reconstruct only from committed events.

## End-to-end outcome

After this walkthrough you should be able to:

- Explain why “dirty” means provisional, not merely incorrect.
- Trace a dirty read from an uncommitted buffer through an application decision and optional cache fan-out.
- Name Read Committed as the isolation floor that closes the anomaly.
- Distinguish engines that cannot emit dirty reads from those that can at `READ UNCOMMITTED` / `NOLOCK`.
- Choose intentional approximate reads without putting them on financial or inventory paths.

## Alternatives considered

**Exclusive locking for every read.** Waiting on the writer’s exclusive lock prevents dirty reads without MVCC, but read throughput collapses under write contention.

**Always Serializable.** Removes dirty reads and most other anomalies, at the cost of higher abort/retry rates that many OLTP APIs are not prepared to handle.

**RCSI or native MVCC at Read Committed.** Preferred alternative to `NOLOCK`: non-blocking readers that still see only committed versions.

## Failure and degraded modes

**Phantom refunds and double credits.** A payment path refunds against an in-flight debit that later rolls back, leaving both the restored balance and the refund.

**Lost sales and poisoned audits.** Checkout reads a provisional zero stock, turns away a buyer, and records a stock-out that never existed after rollback.

**Cache poisoning.** A short dirty observation is stored with a multi-minute TTL and keeps serving the phantom after the database has already healed.

## Key learnings

- A dirty read is acting on a provisional write that may still roll back — the danger is the decision, cache, or event that escapes, not only the row value.
- Read Committed is the isolation floor that forbids dirty reads; it is the default on PostgreSQL, Oracle, and SQL Server.
- PostgreSQL and Oracle cannot emit dirty reads by design; MySQL and SQL Server can at READ UNCOMMITTED, and SQL Server often does via NOLOCK.
- Prefer RCSI or native MVCC committed reads over NOLOCK when you need non-blocking readers without provisional data.
- Use READ UNCOMMITTED only for explicitly approximate analytics — never for payments, inventory commitments, compliance logs, or authoritative caches.

record.summary: A deep production scenario drill diagnosing a critical database CPU spike caused by full table scans and high-cardinality Key Lookups across 120 million rows. Follow how query engineers analyze execution plans, restructure composite key column order, and deploy a zero-downtime covering index to reduce p99 latency from 12,400ms to 1.8ms.

useCase.goal: Eliminate database CPU saturation (98%) and connection pool exhaustion on a high-throughput merchant payments ledger by replacing full table scans and Key Lookups with covering B-Tree index seeks.
requirements: Sub-5ms p99 query latency on transaction lookup queries
Database CPU utilization maintained under 25% at 25,000 queries per second
Zero table write locks and zero application downtime during index deployment
Consistent execution plans without optimizer tipping point regression
constraints: Transactions ledger contains 120,000,000 rows across 2.4 TB NVMe disk storage
Write ingestion rate of 2,200 financial transactions per second must not be degraded
Strict financial compliance prohibits caching sensitive ledger states in unencrypted ephemeral caches
assumptions: PostgreSQL engine with 64 vCPU, 256 GB RAM, and dedicated NVMe SSD storage.
Workload reads filter by merchant_id, status, and created_at date range, ordered by created_at DESC with LIMIT 50.

stages.title: Stage 1: Production Diagnosis & Execution Plan Analysis (EXPLAIN BUFFERS)
stages.decisionOrAction: Execute EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) on the degraded transaction history endpoint to inspect page read volume, operator node costs, and heap memory usage.

conceptRoles.roleDescription: Identifies whether the optimizer selects an Index Seek, Bitmap Index Scan, or Sequential Scan, and measures Key Lookup overhead.

stages.componentBehavior: The execution plan reveals an initial Bitmap Index Scan on a single-column index (idx_transactions_status) matching 4,800,000 rows, followed by a massive Bitmap Heap Scan reading 85,000 disk buffers (680 MB) into RAM to filter by merchant_id and created_at.
stages.observableOutput: Execution time: 12,410ms. Buffer cache read hits: 14,200, disk read misses: 70,800. Query execution causes disk I/O wait spikes and exhausts available database worker threads.

stages.title: Stage 2: Restructuring the Composite Index & Leftmost Prefix Ordering
stages.decisionOrAction: Replace the single-column status index with a composite B-Tree index applying the equality-before-range rule: (merchant_id, status, created_at DESC).

conceptRoles.roleDescription: Enables an exact B-Tree root-to-leaf Index Seek on the high-cardinality merchant_id and status filters.
Leverages B-Tree leaf node bidirectional ordering to satisfy ORDER BY created_at DESC directly without an in-memory Sort operator.

stages.componentBehavior: The optimizer shifts from an O(N) Bitmap Heap Scan to an O(log N) Index Seek. However, because the SELECT query requests transaction_uuid, currency, and amount, the database must perform 50 physical Key Lookups (Heap Fetches) to retrieve non-indexed columns.
stages.observableOutput: Latency drops from 12,410ms to 45ms. While much faster, 50 random single-block page reads still induce disk contention under 25k concurrent QPS, keeping DB CPU at 55%.

stages.title: Stage 3: Architecting the Covering Index with INCLUDE Clause
stages.decisionOrAction: Extend the composite index into a Covering Index by appending non-key projection columns to an INCLUDE clause: (merchant_id, status, created_at DESC) INCLUDE (transaction_uuid, currency, amount).

conceptRoles.roleDescription: Stores payload columns directly in the leaf pages of the secondary B-Tree, completely eliminating Key/Heap Lookups.
Evaluates database buffer cache residency as an in-memory caching tier versus an external Redis cache-aside layer.

stages.componentBehavior: The PostgreSQL query planner selects an 'Index Only Scan'. Because all required fields reside inside the B-Tree leaf node, the engine touches zero table data heap pages. The entire result set is satisfied from 4 page reads in the PostgreSQL buffer cache.
stages.observableOutput: Execution time drops to 1.8ms. Total buffer accesses drop from 85,000 to 4 pages. Zero disk I/O reads required on warm buffer pool.

stages.title: Stage 4: Zero-Downtime Deployment & Write Amplification Guardrails
stages.decisionOrAction: Deploy the index using CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY with monitored maintenance_work_mem, followed by dropping obsolete single-column indexes.

conceptRoles.roleDescription: Builds the two-pass B-Tree index concurrently without acquiring an ExclusiveLock on the table.
Audits write amplification overhead across all secondary indexes to safeguard 2,200 writes/second ingest throughput.

stages.componentBehavior: PostgreSQL executes an initial snapshot scan followed by a validation scan to incorporate in-flight transactions. Dropping redundant status and merchant_id indexes recaptures 45 GB of disk space, offsetting the write overhead of the new covering index.
stages.observableOutput: Zero table locks acquired during the 22-minute index build. Overall insert latency remains constant at 1.4ms with zero application errors.

outcome.endToEndResult: Query latency plummeted from 12,410ms to 1.8ms (a 99.98% speedup). Database CPU dropped from 98% to 14% under 25,000 QPS peak traffic, completely resolving connection pool starvation.
outcome.observedUserBehavior: Merchant dashboard transaction page loads are perceived as instantaneous with zero 504 gateway timeout errors.
outcome.observedOperatorBehavior: Database connection pool queue depth dropped to zero; read replica replication lag decreased from 45 seconds to 0ms.
keyTradeoffs: Index storage overhead (38 GB for the covering index) vs saving 680 MB of buffer cache per query execution.
Small write amplification increase during transaction inserts vs avoiding an expensive multi-node Redis cache-aside infrastructure cluster.

alternatives.title: Redis Cache-Aside Layer for All Transactions
alternatives.explanation: Rejected due to high infrastructure cost (250+ GB RAM needed for financial records), security compliance constraints, and severe cache invalidation race conditions when transactions transition between PENDING, SETTLED, and REFUNDED states.

alternatives.title: Horizontal Database Sharding by Merchant ID
alternatives.explanation: Deferred because architectural sharding introduces distributed transactions, cross-shard query routing complexity, and multi-month migration overhead. Proper covering index tuning delivered the required sub-2ms performance on existing database infrastructure.

failuresAndDegradedModes.name: Optimizer Tipping Point Reversion on Broad Date Filters
failuresAndDegradedModes.behavior: If a merchant requests a 12-month date range matching >20% of their records, the query planner may revert to a sequential scan. Mitigated by enforcing client-side query pagination bounds (max 30-day window per request).

failuresAndDegradedModes.name: Buffer Pool Cold Cache Misses After Instance Failover
failuresAndDegradedModes.behavior: Immediately after an Aurora / RDS failover, read latency temporarily increases to 15-25ms until index leaf pages are paged from NVMe storage into RAM. Mitigated by pre-warming buffer cache using pg_prewarm on critical covering indexes.

record.markdownContent:
## 🚀 Scenario Context: The 12-Second Database Bottleneck

At 09:15 UTC on Cyber Monday, the merchant dashboard for a global fintech platform processing 25,000 queries per second began experiencing catastrophic degradation. The primary merchant ledger table—holding **120 million rows** across **2.4 TB** of NVMe storage—saw its p99 query latency surge from 25ms to **12,400ms**. 

Application connection poolers (PgBouncer) rapidly exhausted their max client pools, cascading into HTTP 504 Gateway Timeouts across merchant APIs. Database CPU pegged at **98%**, dominated by memory buffer scans and disk I/O wait.

The culprit was a high-frequency query powering the merchant transaction reconciliation view:

```sql
SELECT transaction_uuid, created_at, status, amount, currency
FROM transactions
WHERE merchant_id = 'm_8849102'
  AND status = 'COMPLETED'
  AND created_at >= '2026-10-01 00:00:00'
ORDER BY created_at DESC
LIMIT 50;
```

---

## 🔍 Stage 1: Dissecting the Execution Plan (EXPLAIN ANALYZE)

Running `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)` on the unoptimized query revealed why the database was collapsing:

```text
Limit (cost=45120.10..45120.22 rows=50 width=88) (actual time=12408.12..12409.84 rows=50 loops=1)
  Buffers: shared hit=14200 read=70800
  -> Sort (cost=45120.10..45210.30 rows=36000 width=88) (actual time=12408.11..12408.90 rows=50 loops=1)
       Sort Key: created_at DESC
       Sort Method: top-N heapsort  Memory: 38kB
       -> Bitmap Heap Scan on transactions (cost=1200.40..43800.10 rows=36000 width=88) (actual time=450.20..11890.30 rows=38200 loops=1)
            Recheck Cond: (status = 'COMPLETED')
            Filter: ((created_at >= '2026-10-01') AND (merchant_id = 'm_8849102'))
            Rows Removed by Filter: 4761800
            Buffers: shared hit=14200 read=70800
            -> Bitmap Index Scan on idx_transactions_status (cost=0.00..1190.20 rows=4800000 width=0) (actual time=380.10..380.10 rows=4800000 loops=1)
Execution Time: 12410.22 ms
```

### The Failure Mechanics:
1. **Poor Index Selectivity**: The table had only an index on `status`. Because `status = 'COMPLETED'` represented 60% of the entire table, the B-Tree index scan matched 4.8 million rows.
2. **Catastrophic Bitmap Heap Scan**: The database had to load **85,000 pages (680 MB)** from disk to check whether each row belonged to `merchant_id = 'm_8849102'`. 4,761,800 rows were read and immediately discarded by the heap filter!
3. **Memory Sort Overhead**: Because the index was not ordered by `created_at`, the engine had to perform an in-memory `Sort Key: created_at DESC` across 38,200 rows.

---

## 🛠️ Stage 2: Applying the Equality-First Composite Index Rule

A composite index must follow the **Equality First, Range Second** principle. By placing equality predicates first, the B-Tree branches guide search directly to the exact merchant and status partition, eliminating millions of irrelevant rows:

```sql
-- Step 1: Create Composite Index with Equality-before-Range ordering
CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_transactions_merchant_status_date 
ON transactions (merchant_id, status, created_at DESC);
```

### Re-evaluating the Plan:

```text
Limit (cost=0.56..185.12 rows=50 width=88) (actual time=0.82..45.10 rows=50 loops=1)
  Buffers: shared hit=12 read=50
  -> Index Scan using idx_transactions_merchant_status_date on transactions (cost=0.56..185.12 rows=50 width=88)
       Index Cond: ((merchant_id = 'm_8849102') AND (status = 'COMPLETED') AND (created_at >= '2026-10-01'))
Execution Time: 45.32 ms
```

### The Remaining Bottleneck: The Key Lookup / Heap Fetch
Latency plummeted from 12,410ms to **45ms** (a 275x improvement). However, examining `Buffers: shared read=50` showed that for each of the 50 rows returned, the engine had to perform a **Key Lookup (Heap Fetch)** to retrieve `transaction_uuid`, `currency`, and `amount`.

At 25,000 requests per second, 50 random single-block reads per query equals **1,250,000 random page reads per second**, still bottlenecking disk I/O and saturating CPU at 55%.

---

## ⚡ Stage 3: Architecting the Covering Index with INCLUDE

To eliminate the Key Lookup entirely, we convert the index into a **Covering Index**. In PostgreSQL and modern SQL engines, the `INCLUDE` clause stores non-filtering payload columns in the leaf pages of the B-Tree without adding them to the upper search tree branches:

```sql
-- Step 2: Build the Covering Composite Index
CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_transactions_covering_v2
ON transactions (
    merchant_id,         -- 1. Equality seek key
    status,              -- 2. Equality seek key
    created_at DESC      -- 3. Range seek key & pre-sorted order
)
INCLUDE (
    transaction_uuid,    -- Leaf payload column
    amount,              -- Leaf payload column
    currency             -- Leaf payload column
);
```

### The Final Execution Plan: Pure Index Only Scan

```text
Limit (cost=0.56..4.12 rows=50 width=88) (actual time=0.04..1.78 rows=50 loops=1)
  Buffers: shared hit=4 read=0
  -> Index Only Scan using idx_transactions_covering_v2 on transactions (cost=0.56..4.12 rows=50 width=88)
       Index Cond: ((merchant_id = 'm_8849102') AND (status = 'COMPLETED') AND (created_at >= '2026-10-01'))
       Heap Fetches: 0
Execution Time: 1.82 ms
```

```architecture
{
  "view": "high-level",
  "title": "Index Only Scan Path vs Heap Key Lookup Path",
  "nodes": [
    { "id": "client", "label": "API Client Query", "type": "client" },
    { "id": "engine", "label": "Query Optimizer (Postgres)", "type": "processor" },
    { "id": "btree", "label": "Covering B-Tree Leaves [INCLUDE: uuid, amt, curr]", "type": "processor" },
    { "id": "heap", "label": "Table Data Heap Pages (2.4 TB Disk)", "type": "database" }
  ],
  "edges": [
    { "from": "client", "to": "engine", "label": "SELECT ... LIMIT 50" },
    { "from": "engine", "to": "btree", "label": "O(log N) Index Seek (4 Pages)" },
    { "from": "btree", "to": "engine", "label": "Returns 100% Columns (Heap Fetches: 0)" },
    { "from": "engine", "to": "heap", "label": "BYPASSED: Zero Heap Reads!", "style": "dashed" }
  ]
}
```

### The Results:
- **`Heap Fetches: 0`**: The table heap on disk was never touched.
- **Buffers**: Total pages accessed dropped from 85,000 pages to just **4 pages** in RAM.
- **Zero Sort Operator**: `created_at DESC` in the index key allowed the engine to stream the first 50 leaf entries directly, satisfying the `LIMIT 50` in **1.82ms**.
- **Database CPU**: Normalized from **98% down to 14%** under peak load.

---

## 📋 Production Key Learnings & Checklist

1. **Check the Buffers First**: When inspecting execution plans, look at `Buffers: read` vs `hit`. A query scanning thousands of shared buffers is doing excessive work, even if its run time looks short on a warm cache.
2. **Eliminate Key Lookups with `INCLUDE`**: Never use `SELECT *` in high-throughput query paths. Explicitly list columns and store projection fields in index leaves via `INCLUDE` to achieve `Index Only Scans` (`Heap Fetches: 0`).
3. **Follow the Rule of Composite Keys**: `(Equality Columns, Range Columns, Sort Columns) INCLUDE (Payload Columns)`.
4. **Build Concurrently in Production**: Always use `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY` in PostgreSQL or `ALGORITHM=INPLACE, LOCK=NONE` in MySQL to avoid locking writes during high-volume production operations.

initialInventory.title: Hybrid Logical Clocks: The Invisible Timekeeper for Causal Consistency

record.title: Hybrid Logical Clocks: The Invisible Timekeeper for Causal Consistency
record.subtitle: Guaranteeing causal write order in multi-region key-value stores with bounded metadata and local tick operations.
record.summary: How distributed databases enforce strict causal consistency across asynchronous nodes without relying on expensive atomic GPS clocks or unbounded vector clocks.

useCase.goal: Guarantee deterministic causal consistency for multi-region writes without global physical clock synchronization.
requirements: Monotonicity: Timestamps must never move backward on any local node.
Causal ordering: If event A causally precedes event B (A → B), then HLC(A) < HLC(B).
Bounded physical drift: The physical component of HLC tracks physical time within a bounded error ε.
Bounded metadata: Fixed-size 128-bit timestamp tuple <physical_ms, logical_counter>.
constraints: Nodes run on commodity cloud instances subject to standard NTP drift up to 100ms.
Cross-region network partitions and message delays up to 250ms must not corrupt causal ordering.
assumptions: Physical clocks synchronize via NTP with a maximum bounded drift ε ≤ 100ms.

stages.title: Stage 1 — The HLC Coordinate & Tuple Invariant
stages.decisionOrAction: Represent every timestamp as a two-part coordinate <physical_ms, logical_counter> tracking wall-clock time and causal precedence.

conceptRoles.roleDescription: Provides the total order timestamp metadata needed for conflict-free replica convergence.

stages.componentBehavior: The storage engine attaches a 64-bit millisecond physical epoch and a 64-bit integer counter to every write record.
stages.observableOutput: A compact 16-byte metadata header on all mutation records that preserves total causal ordering.

stages.title: Stage 2 — Local Event Tick & Message Receive Rules
stages.decisionOrAction: Execute local tick on new writes and merge remote timestamps upon receiving replication payloads.

conceptRoles.roleDescription: Ensures every node advances its logical state deterministically without inter-region lock waiting.

stages.componentBehavior: On write, if the local physical clock matches the current HLC physical time, increment counter; otherwise reset counter to 0. On message receive, take the maximum physical time and bump the counter if physical clocks coincide.
stages.observableOutput: Deterministically increasing HLC values across all regional write events.

stages.title: Stage 3 — Causal Merging & CRDT Integration
stages.decisionOrAction: Merge concurrent writes deterministically at read time using HLC total order as the tie-breaker.

conceptRoles.roleDescription: Enforces deterministic partition convergence across sharded multi-master partitions.

stages.componentBehavior: When clients issue read-your-own-writes queries, the storage layer compares HLC timestamps to ensure causally newer values supersede older replicas.
stages.observableOutput: Deterministic causal visibility without lost updates or ghost reads across regions.

outcome.endToEndResult: The multi-region KV store achieves deterministic causal consistency with fixed-size 16-byte metadata and zero inter-node wait latency on writes.
outcome.observedUserBehavior: Clients observe strictly monotonic reads and causal read-your-own-writes guarantees regardless of which regional replica serves their request.
outcome.observedOperatorBehavior: Operators verify that physical clock drift remains within bounded threshold ε using metric alerts; no expensive GPS atomic hardware required.
keyTradeoffs: HLC guarantees causal ordering (A → B implies HLC(A) < HLC(B)), but concurrent writes (A || B) are arbitrarily tie-broken by node ID.
Physical clock drift must be bounded by ε; extreme clock skew requires safety throttling or node isolation.
Fixed 16-byte metadata avoids the O(N) network bloat of vector clocks at the cost of loose real-time coupling.

alternatives.title: Google TrueTime (Spanner)
alternatives.explanation: Uses GPS receivers and atomic clocks in each datacenter with commit-wait to guarantee strict external serializability; requires dedicated custom hardware.

alternatives.title: Vector Clocks
alternatives.explanation: Captures the exact causal DAG with zero physical clock dependence, but metadata grows linearly O(N) with the number of nodes, bloating replication payloads.

alternatives.title: Lamport Logical Clocks
alternatives.explanation: Pure monotonic integer counters guarantee causality but drift arbitrarily far from wall-clock time, making time-range queries impossible.

failuresAndDegradedModes.name: Physical Clock Drift Exceeding Bound (Δ > ε)
failuresAndDegradedModes.behavior: If an NTP daemon stalls and a node drifts past the physical error bound ε, the node pauses write acceptance to prevent generating timestamps too far in the future.

failuresAndDegradedModes.name: NTP Backward Clock Step
failuresAndDegradedModes.behavior: If NTP abruptly adjusts physical time backward, the HLC freezes its physical component at the highest observed value and increments the logical counter, preventing backward time travel.

statedAssumptions: Logical physical clock coordination derived from Kulkarni et al. (Logical Physical Clocks and Consistent Snapshots in Globally Distributed Databases).

record.title: Key Terms in Distributed Systems: The Definitive Glossary
record.subtitle: A staged vocabulary walkthrough from interview write-skew to replication, sharding, and consensus
record.summary: Follow one system-design interview from a vague multi-leader proposal through the exact anomalies, isolation levels, replication models, shard-key choices, and consensus rules that make the design defensible.

useCase.goal: Give a learner a precise vocabulary so an interview answer and a production design name the same anomaly, the same isolation guarantee, and the same replication or consensus trade-off.
requirements: Name the anomaly the design actually permits before proposing a fix.
Map each term to one mechanism: snapshot, quorum, shard key, or leader election.
State what an operator can observe when the guarantee holds or fails.
constraints: The feed is globally distributed and accepts writes in more than one region.
Default isolation on the primary is Read Committed unless the design raises it.
Cross-shard transactions are not free and must be called out explicitly.
assumptions: The candidate has already sketched multi-leader replication for a social feed.
The interviewer is testing vocabulary precision, not a blank-page architecture.
Production claims below are teaching reconstructions of well-known mechanisms, pending editorial review.

stages.title: Stage 1 — How Vocabulary Breaks System Design Interviews (and Production Systems)
stages.decisionOrAction: Stop the multi-leader feed design and name the exact anomaly the interviewer asked about: write skew, not a generic consistency problem.

conceptRoles.roleDescription: Forces the high-level design to use one term per failure mode so the rest of the interview can be traced to a mechanism.

stages.componentBehavior: The interviewer pauses after the multi-leader proposal and asks how the design prevents write skew. The candidate must restate the invariant (two writers each pass a shared check, then write non-overlapping rows) before choosing a control.
stages.observableOutput: The answer names write skew, distinguishes it from dirty reads and lost updates, and commits to a concrete control (serializable isolation or an explicit lock row) instead of saying the system will be eventually consistent.

stages.title: Stage 2 — Consistency Anomalies: The Ways Transactions Can Lie to You
stages.decisionOrAction: Classify the feed bug as one anomaly from the standard set: dirty read, non-repeatable read, phantom, read skew, write skew, lost update, or dirty write.

conceptRoles.roleDescription: Supplies the anomaly catalog the design must rule in or out before isolation is chosen.

stages.componentBehavior: Two concurrent sessions read the same on-call or inventory predicate, each concludes the constraint still holds, and each writes a different row. Neither statement conflicts at the row lock, so both commits succeed and the predicate is false.
stages.observableOutput: A post-commit query shows the invariant broken (zero doctors on call, or two bookings of one seat) even though each transaction's own reads looked correct.

stages.title: Stage 3 — Isolation Levels: PostgreSQL's Six-Way Dial Between Safety and Speed
stages.decisionOrAction: Raise only the transactions that check a multi-row invariant to Serializable, and keep ordinary single-row updates at Read Committed with row locks.

conceptRoles.roleDescription: Maps ANSI labels to PostgreSQL mechanisms: statement snapshots, transaction snapshots, and serializable snapshot isolation.

stages.componentBehavior: Read Committed gives each statement a fresh snapshot, so two selects in one transaction can disagree. Repeatable Read freezes the snapshot but still allows write skew. Serializable tracks read-write dependencies and aborts one transaction with SQLSTATE 40001.
stages.observableOutput: The on-call update either commits alone or the second session retries after 40001 and then sees that the last on-call doctor is already off, so it refuses the second checkout.

stages.title: Stage 4 — Replication Models and the Consistency Spectrum Across Databases
stages.decisionOrAction: Choose single-leader synchronous replication for the feed's authoritative writes, and treat multi-leader as an explicit conflict-resolution design rather than a latency shortcut.

conceptRoles.roleDescription: Defines who accepts writes and which replicas must acknowledge them before the client is told the write succeeded.

stages.componentBehavior: A single leader orders writes and ships the log. Synchronous followers block the ack until a quorum has the record. Asynchronous followers return early and can lose the tail on failover. Multi-leader and leaderless modes accept writes on more than one node and must reconcile divergent versions.
stages.observableOutput: After the client receives a success, a failover or a read from another replica still returns the new post, or the design documents the window where a replica can lag or diverge.

stages.title: Stage 5 — Partitioning and Sharding: Distributing Data Across Nodes
stages.decisionOrAction: Shard the feed by a high-cardinality immutable key that matches the dominant query, and refuse a timestamp or auto-increment key that piles every new write onto one shard.

conceptRoles.roleDescription: Decides which node owns a row and which queries stay local versus scatter-gather.

stages.componentBehavior: The router hashes or ranges the shard key and sends the write to one shard. Queries that include the key hit one node. Queries that omit it fan out, wait for the slowest shard, and merge. Changing the shard count with modulo hashing moves almost every row; consistent hashing moves about 1/N.
stages.observableOutput: A user timeline read hits one shard in single-digit milliseconds, while a global 'latest posts' query is either served from a purpose-built index or is visibly a scatter-gather with a documented latency budget.

stages.title: Stage 6 — Consensus and Leader Election: Deciding Who Gets the Final Say
stages.decisionOrAction: Use a consensus protocol for the shard map and the replication leader, and do not let application nodes elect a leader with a single timeout and a last-write-wins clock.

conceptRoles.roleDescription: Requires a quorum to agree on one leader and one log order before a configuration or write is committed.

stages.componentBehavior: Followers vote in a term. A candidate becomes leader only with a majority. The leader replicates log entries and commits them once a majority has stored them. A partitioned minority cannot commit, which prevents split brain at the cost of unavailability.
stages.observableOutput: Operators see one leader per term, committed log indexes that never go backwards, and a minority partition that rejects writes instead of accepting a second history.

outcome.endToEndResult: The same vocabulary now drives both the interview answer and the production controls: name the anomaly, pick the isolation or replication rule that closes it, place data with a shard key that matches the query, and elect one leader with a quorum.
outcome.observedUserBehavior: Readers and writers see either a committed post that survives failover or an explicit retry, never a silent double-booking or a second history.
outcome.observedOperatorBehavior: Dashboards show isolation aborts, replication lag, hot shards, and leader terms as separate signals instead of one 'consistency' alert.
keyTradeoffs: Serializable closes write skew but requires retry handling for SQLSTATE 40001.
Synchronous replication removes the lost-tail window and adds ack latency.
A query-aligned shard key makes the primary path local and pushes secondary access patterns onto indexes.
Quorum consensus prevents split brain and refuses writes when a majority is unreachable.

alternatives.title: Stay on Read Committed and lock the predicate
alternatives.explanation: For a single hot row, SELECT FOR UPDATE is enough and avoids serialization retries. It does not close write skew across two different rows unless you also lock a shared sentinel row.

alternatives.title: Multi-leader with last-write-wins
alternatives.explanation: Cuts cross-region write latency but turns conflicts into silent overwrites. Use it only when the product can name the conflict rule and the data that may be discarded.

failuresAndDegradedModes.name: Write skew under snapshot isolation
failuresAndDegradedModes.behavior: Both sessions commit. The shared invariant is false only after both commits. Detection is a constraint query after the fact, or a 40001 abort if the transaction ran at Serializable.

failuresAndDegradedModes.name: Hot shard from a monotonic key
failuresAndDegradedModes.behavior: The newest range absorbs every insert. Cluster throughput collapses to that one node's capacity. Mitigation is a hashed or compound key, or pre-split ranges with monitoring on the tail.

failuresAndDegradedModes.name: Minority partition during leader election
failuresAndDegradedModes.behavior: The minority cannot gather a quorum, so it rejects writes. Clients retry against the majority leader. Accepting those writes would fork the log.

record.markdownContent:
## Stage 1 — How Vocabulary Breaks System Design Interviews (and Production Systems)

You are 35 minutes into a system design interview. You have just proposed multi-leader replication for a globally distributed social feed. The interviewer pauses and says: "Your design doesn't account for write skew. Walk me through how you'd prevent it."

A nod is not an answer. Write skew is a specific interleaving: two transactions each read an overlapping predicate, each decides the constraint still holds, and each writes a **different** row. No single-row lock fires. Both commits succeed. The predicate the product promised — at least one doctor on call, one seat left, one canonical post id — is now false.

That is different from a dirty read (you saw an uncommitted write that later vanished), a lost update (two read-modify-writes hit the **same** row and one overwrote the other), and "eventual consistency" (replicas have not caught up yet). If the answer uses those phrases interchangeably, the interviewer cannot tell which mechanism you would actually ship.

The decision in this stage is to freeze the design and name the anomaly before picking a database feature. The component that must change is the candidate's next sentence, not the diagram. The observable output is a sentence of the form: "Two writers can each pass the on-call check and update different rows; I will close that with Serializable isolation or a shared lock row, not with multi-leader replication."

The same failure shows up in production incident reviews. A ticket titled "inconsistent data" hides three different bugs and three different fixes. Vocabulary is the routing key for the rest of this scenario.

## Stage 2 — Consistency Anomalies: The Ways Transactions Can Lie to You

Once the anomaly has a name, classify it against the catalog. Each row below is a different lie the database can tell a transaction, and each lie has a different business symptom.

| Anomaly | What the transaction observes | What the product ships |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Dirty read | A value that another transaction has not committed and may roll back | A decision based on state that never existed |
| Non-repeatable read | Two selects of the same row in one transaction return different committed values | A branch taken on a number that is already stale |
| Phantom read | A range query grows or shrinks inside one transaction | A constraint check that passed on an incomplete set |
| Read skew | Two related rows are read from different points in time | A transfer that looks balanced in neither account |
| Write skew | Two transactions each pass a shared check and write non-overlapping rows | Double booking, empty on-call roster |
| Lost update | Two read-modify-writes of the same row; one write disappears | A balance incremented once instead of twice |
| Dirty write | A second transaction overwrites an uncommitted first write | A row whose history cannot be reconstructed |

The on-call example is write skew, not a lost update. Alice reads `count(on_call) = 2` and sets her own row to off. Bob does the same for his row. Neither update touches the other's row, so Read Committed and snapshot isolation both allow both commits. A later `count(on_call)` returns 0.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant Alice
    participant DB
    participant Bob
    Alice->>DB: BEGIN snapshot
    Bob->>DB: BEGIN snapshot
    Alice->>DB: count on_call
    DB-->>Alice: 2
    Bob->>DB: count on_call
    DB-->>Bob: 2
    Alice->>DB: set Alice off
    Bob->>DB: set Bob off
    Alice->>DB: COMMIT
    Bob->>DB: COMMIT
    Note over DB: Invariant broken: zero doctors on call
```

The decision is to pick one row from that table and refuse the others. The component behavior is the interleaving above. The observable output is a query after both commits that shows the invariant false — proof you named the right anomaly.

## Stage 3 — Isolation Levels: PostgreSQL's Six-Way Dial Between Safety and Speed

Isolation is the dial that decides which rows from the previous table are still possible. PostgreSQL does not implement Read Uncommitted; that setting is promoted to Read Committed. The levels you actually choose among are Read Committed, Repeatable Read, and Serializable.

Read Committed takes a **new snapshot per statement**. Two selects of `balance` inside one transaction can return 100 and then 50 if another transaction committed in between. That is a non-repeatable read. It is the default, and it is the right default for single-statement work. It does not protect check-then-act logic.

Repeatable Read takes **one snapshot for the transaction**. The same row keeps the same value, and PostgreSQL's MVCC visibility rules also hide phantoms that were inserted after the snapshot. It still allows write skew, because each transaction's snapshot cannot see the other transaction's concurrent write to a different row.

Serializable in PostgreSQL is serializable snapshot isolation. Transactions still run on snapshots, but the engine records read-write dependencies. When Alice's read depends on a row Bob writes and Bob's read depends on a row Alice writes, one commit is aborted with `SQLSTATE 40001`. The survivor stays. The aborted session must retry; on retry it sees the updated count and refuses to go off call.

```sql
BEGIN TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL SERIALIZABLE;
SELECT count(*) FROM on_call
  WHERE shift = current_date AND status = 'active';
-- application: proceed only when count > 1
UPDATE on_call
   SET status = 'off'
 WHERE doctor_id = $1 AND shift = current_date;
COMMIT;
```

The decision is not "turn Serializable on for the whole pool." Ordinary single-row updates stay at Read Committed, often with `SELECT … FOR UPDATE` on the row they will change. Only the multi-row predicate — on-call count, remaining seats across a cabin, inventory across warehouses — moves to Serializable, and the service retries `40001` with backoff.

Oracle's label "Serializable" is snapshot isolation. It does not give you this abort. If the design says "we set serializable," the observable output must name the engine: a PostgreSQL `40001` in the logs, or an explicit lock row if the engine cannot detect the cycle.

## Stage 4 — Replication Models and the Consistency Spectrum Across Databases

Isolation answers what one node lets concurrent transactions see. Replication answers what **another node** is allowed to serve after the client was told the write succeeded.

Single-leader replication gives one node the right to order writes and ships that log to followers. Synchronous replication waits until a configured set of followers has the record before the leader acks the client. A failover then has the write. Asynchronous replication acks from the leader alone. It is faster, and a crash can drop the tail that followers never received. Readers on a lagging follower can also miss the write; that is replica lag, not write skew.

Multi-leader replication lets more than one node accept writes, usually one leader per region. Conflicts are inevitable when the same key is written in two places. Last-write-wins is a policy for discarding one of them, not a proof that both happened. Use it only when the product can say which value may disappear.

Leaderless replication (the Dynamo family) lets any replica accept a write and reconciles with quorums and read repair. A write quorum `W` and a read quorum `R` with `W + R > N` overlap, so a read sees the latest write if no node is missing from both sets. If `W + R ≤ N`, a read can miss a write that succeeded. That is a different knob from isolation level, and interview answers that mix them are answering two questions with one word.

The decision for the social feed's authoritative post record is single-leader synchronous replication (or a quorum that overlaps reads and writes). Multi-leader is allowed only for data whose conflict rule is written down. The observable output is: after the client sees success, a promoted follower or a quorum read returns the new post, and replication lag is a separate metric from serialization failures.

## Stage 5 — Partitioning and Sharding: Distributing Data Across Nodes

Replication copies the **same** data so you can survive a node loss and spread reads. Sharding splits the data so no single node holds every row or absorbs every write. The shard key is the column the router uses to choose a node. It is expensive to change later because every row may have to move.

A useful key has high cardinality, spreads writes, matches the query you run most often, and does not change for the life of the row. `user_id` on a timeline does that: one user's posts live together, and writes from many users spread out. `created_at` looks high-cardinality and still sends every insert to the newest shard. `country_code` is easy to explain and creates a permanent hot shard for the largest country.

Range sharding keeps order, so a between-query can stay on one shard, and it creates a hot tail when keys increase monotonically. Hash sharding spreads sequential keys and turns every range scan into a scatter-gather. Consistent hashing keeps most keys in place when you add a node: about `1/N` of the data moves, especially with virtual nodes. A directory (shard map) lets you place a celebrity key on its own node, and the map itself becomes a dependency that must stay available.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  Client --> Router
  Router -->|user_id hash| S0[Shard 0]
  Router -->|user_id hash| S1[Shard 1]
  Router -->|no shard key| Fanout[Scatter-gather]
  Fanout --> S0
  Fanout --> S1
```

The decision is to shard the feed by `user_id` (or a compound tenant plus user key) with hashing or consistent hashing, and to serve "latest across everyone" from a separate index rather than from a scatter on the primary table. The observable output is a timeline read that touches one shard, plus a dashboard query whose plan shows N shard round-trips if someone forgot the key.

## Stage 6 — Consensus and Leader Election: Deciding Who Gets the Final Say

Sharding and replication both assume someone knows which node is the leader and which shard owns a key. If two nodes both believe they are leader, you get two histories. Clocks do not settle that argument: "latest timestamp" is another last-write-wins policy, and clocks drift.

Consensus protocols (Raft is the one most teams can walk through) elect one leader per term and replicate a log. A candidate needs votes from a majority. A log entry is committed only after a majority has stored it. A partition that holds only a minority cannot elect a leader and cannot commit. Clients in that partition see errors and retry. That unavailability is the mechanism that prevents split brain.

The same rule applies to the shard map. If the map is updated by a single node without a quorum, a stale router can send writes to a shard that no longer owns the key. Leader election for the database and quorum agreement for the map are the same idea: a majority must agree before the configuration is real.

Do not implement "whoever heartbeats last wins" in application code. The decision is to put leader election and the shard map on a consensus system (the database's own Raft group, or a dedicated one) and to surface the term and commit index. The observable output is one leader per term, a commit index that does not move backwards, and a minority partition that rejects writes instead of accepting a second log.

## Key learnings

- Name the anomaly before you name the feature. Write skew, lost update, replica lag, and split brain are four different bugs.
- Read Committed and Repeatable Read do not close write skew. PostgreSQL Serializable does, and the application must retry `40001`.
- Replication chooses who may ack a write. Sharding chooses which node stores it. Consensus chooses who is allowed to decide either of those facts.
- A shard key is a query-locality decision. A monotonic key with range sharding creates a hot shard no amount of replication will fix.
- A minority partition that still accepts writes has already forked history. Quorum refusal is the correct degraded mode.

## Scenario context

AI is a tool, not a religion. Use **Code** for deterministic logic (banking, math). Use **Traditional ML** for structured predictions (fraud, recommendations). Use **LLMs** for unstructured text (summarization, chat). Use **Agents** only when a task genuinely requires multi-step planning and external tool calls.

---

Choosing the right approach starts by analyzing your problem's input structure, output requirements…

This walkthrough focuses on **The Decision Flow: From Problem to Paradigm**.

Before making a design choice, clarify:

- Choosing the right approach starts by analyzing your problem's input structure, output requirements, and tolerance for non-determinism.

**Concepts in play:** llm-agents-and-langgraph, deep-learning-foundations, event-driven-architecture, hash-tables-and-bloom-filters

## Stage 1 — One Codebase, Four Paradigms: Know Before You Reach for the LLM

- The most expensive mistake in modern software is using an LLM for a problem deterministic code solves in 5 lines.
- Before adding an AI component, ask two questions: 1.
- Does the input have known structure?
- If both answers are no and the input is natural language, then LLMs are the right tool.

*Applies **llm-agents-and-langgraph** to the decision above.*

**Observable outcome:** If both answers are no and the input is natural language, then LLMs are the right tool.

## Stage 2 — Deep Dive: The Four Paradigms at a Glance

- A quick reference before diving deeper.
- Each paradigm has a distinct role — picking the wrong one costs time, money, and unnecessary complexity.
- Think of it as a filter: start at Code and only move down the list when the previous paradigm genuinely cannot handle the problem.

*Applies **deep-learning-foundations** to the decision above.*

**Observable outcome:** Think of it as a filter: start at Code and only move down the list when the previous paradigm genuinely cannot handle the problem.

## Stage 3 — Pure Code: When Determinism Is Non-Negotiable

- Any operation where you can write an explicit rule belongs here.
- When code beats AI: Banking transactions, data migrations, format validation, mathematical computations, protocol parsing.
- The rule: if a junior developer could write a test that covers every case, write code.

*Applies **event-driven-architecture** to the decision above.*

**Observable outcome:** The rule: if a junior developer could write a test that covers every case, write code.

## Stage 4 — Traditional ML: Patterns in Structured Tabular Data

- Use ML when the rule is too complex to write by hand, but the input is structured (rows and columns with known features).
- ML requires: labeled training data, feature engineering, model evaluation, and a retraining pipeline.
- If you don't have those, use rules instead.

*Applies **hash-tables-and-bloom-filters** to the decision above.*

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    Features[Structured Features age, amount, location] --> Model[ML Model XGBoost / Random Forest]
    Model --> Prediction[Score or Label fraud probability]
```

**Observable outcome:** If you don't have those, use rules instead.

## Stage 5 — Deep Dive: LLMs: When the Input Is Unstructured Text

- LLMs excel at tasks where the input is free-form text and the output is also text (or a structured schema derived from text).
- Cost reminder: Every LLM call costs money and adds latency.
- Never use an LLM for tasks that code or a simple ML model can solve.
- 🔬 Internals Traditional software follows deterministic control flow: the same input always produces the same output via explicit conditional branches.

*Applies **llm-agents-and-langgraph** to the decision above.*

**Observable outcome:** 🔬 Internals Traditional software follows deterministic control flow: the same input always produces the same output via explicit conditional branches.

## Stage 6 — Agents: For Multi-Step Goals That Require External Tools

- Use agents when completing the task requires: 1.
- Multiple actions (not just one generation) 2.
- Calling external APIs or tools (not just text transformation) 3.
- Adapting plans based on intermediate results Red flag: If you're describing your agent as "it just generates text and returns it," you needed a plain LLM call, not an agent.

*Applies **deep-learning-foundations** to the decision above.*

**Observable outcome:** Adapting plans based on intermediate results Red flag: If you're describing your agent as "it just generates text and returns it," you needed a plain LLM call, not an agent.

## End-to-end outcome

Choosing the right approach starts by analyzing your problem's input structure, output requirements, and tolerance for non-determinism.

## Alternatives considered

### Decision Guide: Choosing the Right Tool

The flowchart below turns the two intro questions into a repeatable process you can run mentally for any new backlog item.

### HuggingFace Transformers & scikit-learn: LLM Inference vs Traditional ML Pipeline Side by Side

HuggingFace Transformers is the go-to Python library for loading and running open-source LLMs (GPT-2, LLaMA, Mistral).


## Failure and degraded modes

### Trade-offs & Failure Modes: When Each Paradigm Breaks Down

- **Detection:** This flowchart maps any new requirement through a four-question decision tree that routes it to the right paradigm.

record.markdownContent:
## Scenario context

A vector database stores meaning as numbers so you can search by intent, not exact keywords. That is why "reset my password" can find "account recovery steps" even if the words are different.

---






```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Raw Documents] --> B[Chunking]
    B --> C[Embedding Model]
    C --> D[Vector + Metadata]
    D --> E[ANN Index]
    Q[User Query] --> R[Query Embedding]
    R --> E
    E --> S[Top-k C…

This walkthrough focuses on **How the RAG Pipeline Connects Every Piece**.

Before making a design choice, clarify:

- The most common production pattern is Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) , where the vector database acts as the LLM's long-term memory.
- Without the vector database the LLM only knows what was in its training data.
- With it, the model can cite your private knowledge base, product catalog, or today's incidents.

**Concepts in play:** vector-databases-rag, database-indexing, sorting-and-searching-algorithms, vector-embeddings-and-similarity

## Stage 1 — Deep Dive: ANN Index Structures

- ANN (Approximate Nearest Neighbor) indexes make vector search fast at scale by trading a tiny amount of recall for dramatically lower query latency: Pinecone and Weaviate default to HNSW.
- Chroma uses HNSW via hnswlib .
- pgvector supports both HNSW and IVF.
- 🔬 Internals Vector databases index high-dimensional embeddings using Approximate Nearest Neighbor (ANN) algorithms.

*Applies **vector-databases-rag** to the decision above.*

**Observable outcome:** 🔬 Internals Vector databases index high-dimensional embeddings using Approximate Nearest Neighbor (ANN) algorithms.

## Stage 2 — Real-World Application: Semantic Search for a Support Knowledge Base

- Scenario: Your support team has 50,000 help articles.
- Customers type questions in natural language and expect the right article — even when wording does not match any article title.
- Step 1 — Index: Chunk each article into 400-token segments.
- Embed each chunk with text-embedding-ada-002 .

*Applies **database-indexing** to the decision above.*

**Observable outcome:** Embed each chunk with text-embedding-ada-002 .

## Stage 3 — Your First Semantic Search with Chroma in Python

- Chroma is the fastest way to try a vector database locally — no signup, no cluster, one pip install .
- What happens under the hood: Chroma embeds the documents and query using all-MiniLM-L6-v2 , stores them in an HNSW index, and returns the nearest vectors by cosine distance.
- To go to production, swap chromadb.Client() for Pinecone or Weaviate and use text-embedding-ada-002 .

*Applies **sorting-and-searching-algorithms** to the decision above.*

```python
import chromadb

client = chromadb.Client()
collection = client.create_collection("support-docs")

# Index two documents (Chroma embeds them with its built-in model)
collection.add(
    documents=[
        "How to reset your account password via email link",
        "Steps to recover access when two-factor authentication is lost",
    ],
    ids=["doc-1", "doc-2"],
)

# Query with a natural-language question
results = collection.query(
    query_texts=["I can't log in, forgot my credentials"],
    n_results=2,
)

for doc, dist in zip(results["documents"][0], results["distances"][0]):
    print(f"[score {1 - dist:.3f}] {doc[:60]}...")
```

**Observable outcome:** To go to production, swap chromadb.Client() for Pinecone or Weaviate and use text-embedding-ada-002 .

## Stage 4 — ChromaDB, Pinecone, Weaviate, and pgvector: Picking the Right Vector Store

- ChromaDB is an open-source embedded vector database built for local development and rapid prototyping — zero infrastructure required.
- Pinecone is a managed cloud vector database with serverless scaling.
- Weaviate is an open-source vector search engine with native hybrid (BM25 + vector) search.
- pgvector is a PostgreSQL extension that adds vector storage and ANN search without leaving your existing relational database.

*Applies **vector-embeddings-and-similarity** to the decision above.*

```python
# --- ChromaDB + sentence-transformers (local prototype, no signup needed) ---
# pip install chromadb sentence-transformers
import chromadb
from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer

encoder    = SentenceTransformer("all-MiniLM-L6-v2")
client     = chromadb.PersistentClient(path="./chroma_store")
collection = client.get_or_create_collection("knowledge-base")

docs = [
    "Password reset sends a one-time link to your registered email address.",
    "Two-factor authentication can be disabled from your account security settings.",
]
embeddings = encoder.encode(docs).tolist()
collection.upsert(documents=docs, embeddings=embeddings, ids=["doc-1", "doc-2"])

query_vec = encoder.encode(["I forgot my login credentials"]).tolist()
results   = collection.query(query_embeddings=query_vec, n_results=2)
for doc, dist in zip(results["documents"][0], results["distances"][0]):
    print(f"[similarity {1 - dist:.3f}] {doc[:80]}")

# --- pgvector (stays inside Postgres — zero new infrastructure) ---
# pip install psycopg2-binary pgvector
import psycopg2
from pgvector.psycopg2 import register_vector

conn = psycopg2.connect("dbname=support user=postgres")
register_vector(conn)
with conn.cursor() as cur:
    cur.execute("CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS vector")
    cur.execute(
        "CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS docs "
        "(id serial PRIMARY KEY, content text, embedding vector(384))"
    )
    vec = encoder.encode("Password reset guide").tolist()
    cur.execute("INSERT INTO docs (content, embedding) VALUES (%s, %s)",
                ("Password reset guide", vec))
    # Cosine similarity search: <=> is the pgvector cosine distance operator
    query_vec = encoder.encode("forgot credentials").tolist()
    cur.execute(
        "SELECT content, 1 - (embedding <=> %s) AS similarity "
        "FROM docs ORDER BY embedding <=> %s LIMIT 5",
        (query_vec, query_vec)
    )
    for row in cur.fetchall():
        print(f"[similarity {row[1]:.3f}] {row[0]}")
conn.commit()
```

**Observable outcome:** pgvector is a PostgreSQL extension that adds vector storage and ANN search without leaving your existing relational database.

## Stage 5 — Three Things That Catch Every Vector Database Beginner

- You cannot search across mixed embedding models.
- If you index with text-embedding-ada-002 and later query with bge-base-en , the vectors live in incompatible geometric spaces — ANN search returns garbage.
- Use the same model for both indexing and querying, and track which model version was used for each document batch.
- Filtering happens in metadata, not in the vector space.

*Applies **vector-databases-rag** to the decision above.*

record.markdownContent:
## Scenario context

Pre-training is the phase where an LLM learns "Language" and "World Knowledge" by reading petabytes of text. It uses **Self-Supervised Learning** to predict the next word in a sentence. This creates the "Base Model" which is later fine-tuned.

---

Imagine teaching a child to read.

- **Pre-training:** You lock the child in a library for ten years. They read every book — grammar, history, math, code, recipes. They a…

This walkthrough focuses on **The Library Metaphor: What Pre-training Actually Does**.

Before making a design choice, clarify:

- Imagine teaching a child to read.
- - Pre-training: You lock the child in a library for ten years.
- They read every book — grammar, history, math, code, recipes.

**Concepts in play:** deep-learning-foundations, api-gateway, vector-embeddings-and-similarity, database-sharding

## Stage 1 — Deep Dive: Pre-Training Fundamentals

- Before an LLM can write poetry, translate languages, or explain code, it needs to understand the basic patterns of human text.
- Pre-training is the process of building that foundational understanding from scratch — no hand-labeled data required.
- Self-supervised learning is the key insight that makes this scale.
- Instead of asking humans to annotate millions of examples, the model creates its own training signal: given the words so far, predict the next one.

*Applies **deep-learning-foundations** to the decision above.*

**Observable outcome:** Instead of asking humans to annotate millions of examples, the model creates its own training signal: given the words so far, predict the next one.

## Stage 2 — The Pre-Training Workflow: From Raw Data to Base Model

- Pre-training follows a structured pipeline.
- Each stage is essential — skipping or rushing any one of them measurably degrades the final model quality.
- What each stage does: - Dedup + filter: Remove near-duplicate web pages and low-quality HTML.
- Training on repeated text causes the model to memorize rather than generalize.

*Applies **api-gateway** to the decision above.*

```mermaid
graph TD
    A[Raw Text Sources Web  Books  Code  Papers] --> B[Deduplication & Quality Filtering]
    B --> C[Tokenization BPE / SentencePiece]
    C --> D[Packed Sequences Fill Context Windows]
    D --> E[GPU / TPU Cluster Forward Pass + Backpropagation]
    E --> F{Checkpoint?}
    F -->|Every N steps| G[Save Checkpoint to Storage]
    F -->|Continue training| E
    G --> H[Base Model]
```

**Observable outcome:** Training on repeated text causes the model to memorize rather than generalize.

## Stage 3 — Next-Token Prediction: The Self-Supervised Training Signal

- The entire pre-training game is one question repeated billions of times: "Given the text so far, what is the most likely next token?" This is self-supervised because the labels are already in the data — you just mask th…
- The Loss Function: Cross-Entropy $$L = -\sum {t} \log P(x t \mid x {<t})$$ - $x t$: the correct next token at step $t$ - $x {<t}$: all preceding tokens - $P(x t \mid x {<t})$: the model's probability for the correct tok…
- Minimizing $L$ over trillions of tokens forces the model to learn grammar, facts, and reasoning patterns.
- 📊 Next-Token Prediction Training Loop This sequence diagram traces one complete training step from raw text to updated model weights.

*Applies **vector-embeddings-and-similarity** to the decision above.*

```
Input:   "The capital of France is"
Target:  "Paris"
```

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant D as Data Loader
    participant T as Tokenizer
    participant M as Transformer
    participant L as Loss Function
    participant O as Optimizer

    D->>T: Raw text sequence
    T->>M: Token IDs [x1, x2, ..., xN]
    M->>M: Forward pass (attention layers)
    M->>L: Predicted logits for each position
    L->>L: Cross-entropy vs true next token
    L->>O: Backpropagate gradients
    O->>M: Update all weights
    M->>D: Ready for next batch
```

**Observable outcome:** 📊 Next-Token Prediction Training Loop This sequence diagram traces one complete training step from raw text to updated model weights.

## Stage 4 — The Data Pipeline: From the Web to a Training Run

- This pipeline shows the journey from raw internet crawl data to packed training batches ready for a GPU cluster.
- Near-duplicate removal and quality filtering happen early because noisy or repeated text degrades model quality far more than simply adding more volume.
- The final packing step is critical for GPU efficiency: sequences are concatenated to fill each context window completely, ensuring no compute cycles are wasted on padding tokens.
- Training data typically includes Common Crawl (web text), Books3, GitHub code, arXiv papers, and Wikipedia.

*Applies **database-sharding** to the decision above.*

```mermaid



flowchart LR
    A[Common Crawl Books3 / GitHub / arXiv] --> B[Deduplication]
    B --> C[Quality Filtering]
    C --> D[Tokenization]
    D --> E[Packed Sequences 2K128K tokens]
    E --> F[Training Shards on Object Storage]
    F --> G[GPU Cluster]
```

**Observable outcome:** Training data typically includes Common Crawl (web text), Books3, GitHub code, arXiv papers, and Wikipedia.

## Stage 5 — Deep Dive: Inside the Training Loop: Loss, Gradients, and Checkpoints

- The training loop looks like this in pseudocode: In practice, training runs on thousands of GPUs or TPUs for weeks to months, using advanced parallelism strategies (data parallelism, tensor parallelism, pipeline paralle…
- 🔬 Internals Pre-training minimizes cross-entropy loss over next-token prediction: L = -Σ log P(t i t 1,...,t {i-1}).
- The training corpus is tokenized and packed into fixed-length sequences (e.g., 2048 or 4096 tokens); documents are concatenated with separator tokens to maximize GPU utilization.
- Learning rate follows a warmup-then-cosine-decay schedule — warmup prevents early instability; cosine decay improves final perplexity by 2–5%.

*Applies **deep-learning-foundations** to the decision above.*

```python
for batch in training_data:
    tokens = tokenize(batch)
    logits = model(tokens[:-1])          # predict all positions
    loss = cross_entropy(logits, tokens[1:])  # compare to true next token
    loss.backward()                      # compute gradients
    optimizer.step()                     # update weights
    optimizer.zero_grad()
    if step % checkpoint_interval == 0:
        save_checkpoint(model)
```

**Observable outcome:** Learning rate follows a warmup-then-cosine-decay schedule — warmup prevents early instability; cosine decay improves final perplexity by 2–5%.

## Stage 6 — Real-World Applications: Where Pre-trained Models Power the World

- Pre-trained language models are the invisible backbone of dozens of products in use today.
- The same foundational technique — next-token prediction on massive corpora — powers everything from consumer chat apps to scientific research tools.
- Beyond chat assistants, pre-trained models drive progress across many fields: - Search engines: Google and Bing use LLMs to improve query understanding and surface direct answers within results.
- - Legal and finance: Domain-specific models read and summarize contracts, regulatory filings, and earnings calls in seconds.

*Applies **api-gateway** to the decision above.*

**Observable outcome:** - Legal and finance: Domain-specific models read and summarize contracts, regulatory filings, and earnings calls in seconds.

## End-to-end outcome

Imagine teaching a child to read.

## Alternatives considered

### Decision Guide: What a Base Model Can and Cannot Do

A base model will happily continue any text you give it — including harmful content.


## Failure and degraded modes

### Trade-offs & Failure Modes: Cost, Carbon, and Scaling

- **Detection:** Training a frontier-scale LLM (GPT-4, LLaMA 3 70B) requires: - Compute: thousands of H100 GPUs running for months - Cost: $50M–$100M+ per frontier run - Energy: significant carbon footprint The key t…
- **User or operator impact:** Training a frontier-scale LLM (GPT-4, LLaMA 3 70B) requires: - Compute: thousands of H100 GPUs running for months - Cost: $50M–$100M+ per frontier run - Energy: significant carbon footprint The key t…
