## Scenario context

Unsupervised learning helps you find patterns when you do not have labels. Clustering groups similar data points into segments, and dimensionality reduction compresses large feature spaces into smaller, useful representations for visualization, search, and downstream models.

---

Spotify's **"Discover Weekly"** playlist groups listeners into micro-genres like "Indie Stomp and Holler" and "Vapor Twitch" — without an…

This walkthrough focuses on **Finding Structure Where There Are No Labels**.

Before making a design choice, clarify:

- Spotify's "Discover Weekly" playlist groups listeners into micro-genres like "Indie Stomp and Holler" and "Vapor Twitch" — without anyone ever labeling the data.
- Nobody told the algorithm what genres exist or how many to create.
- It found them by clustering millions of listening patterns, discovering structure that nobody had explicitly defined.

**Concepts in play:** deep-learning-foundations, vector-embeddings-and-similarity, sorting-and-searching-algorithms, tree-data-structures

## Stage 1 — The Unsupervised Input: Unlabeled Feature Matrices

- Unsupervised pipelines start with a feature matrix X — rows are examples, columns are features — but no label column exists .
- Toy dataset — user segments: Even without labels, three groups are visible: high-spend frequent users, low-spend infrequent users, and a mid-range group.
- Preprocessing matters: Distance-based methods are sensitive to scale.
- If monthly spend ranges 0–1000 and sessions/week ranges 0–10, spend will dominate Euclidean distance unless features are standardized first.

*Applies **deep-learning-foundations** to the decision above.*

**Observable outcome:** If monthly spend ranges 0–1000 and sessions/week ranges 0–10, spend will dominate Euclidean distance unless features are standardized first.

## Stage 2 — Clustering Algorithms: K-Means, DBSCAN, and Hierarchical

- K-Means alternates two steps until convergence: 1.
- Assign each point to the nearest centroid.
- Recompute each centroid as the mean of its assigned points.
- K-Means minimizes: $$\min {\{c k\}} \sum {i=1}^{n} \ x i - c {k(i)} \ ^2$$ It is fast but assumes roughly spherical clusters and requires choosing $k$ in advance.

*Applies **vector-embeddings-and-similarity** to the decision above.*

**Observable outcome:** K-Means minimizes: $$\min {\{c k\}} \sum {i=1}^{n} \ x i - c {k(i)} \ ^2$$ It is fast but assumes roughly spherical clusters and requires choosing $k$ in advance.

## Stage 3 — Deep Dive: How K-Means Converges Step by Step

- K-Means alternates two steps until assignments stop changing.
- In the assignment step , each point is assigned to the nearest centroid by Euclidean distance.
- In the update step , each centroid moves to the mean of its assigned points.
- Total inertia (within-cluster sum of squares) can only decrease or stay flat each iteration — it never increases — guaranteeing convergence, though not necessarily to the global optimum.

*Applies **sorting-and-searching-algorithms** to the decision above.*

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A[Initialize K Centroids] --> B[Assign Points to Cluster]
    B --> C[Recompute Centroids]
    C --> D{Centroids Changed?}
    D -- Yes --> B
    D -- No --> E[Final Clusters]
```

**Observable outcome:** Total inertia (within-cluster sum of squares) can only decrease or stay flat each iteration — it never increases — guaranteeing convergence, though not necessarily to the global optimum.

## Stage 4 — Dimensionality Reduction: PCA, t-SNE, and Autoencoders

- PCA (Principal Component Analysis): - Linear technique — finds the directions of maximum variance in the data.
- - Great baseline for tabular numeric data.
- - "Variance captured by first 2 components = 87%" is easy to communicate.
- t-SNE and UMAP: - Non-linear embeddings that preserve neighborhood relationships.

*Applies **tree-data-structures** to the decision above.*

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Raw Unlabeled Data] --> B[Clean and Scale Features]
    B --> C{Goal?}
    C -->|Grouping| D[Run Clustering]
    C -->|Compression or Viz| E[Run Dimensionality Reduction]
    D --> F[Validate Cluster Quality]
    E --> G[Validate Information Retention]
    F --> H[Business Interpretation]
    G --> H
```

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[High-Dim Data] --> B[Standardize Features]
    B --> C[Compute Covariance Matrix]
    C --> D[Eigen Decomposition]
    D --> E[Sort Eigenvectors]
    E --> F[Select Top K Vectors]
    F --> G[Project Data]
    G --> H[Reduced Dimensions]
```

**Observable outcome:** t-SNE and UMAP: - Non-linear embeddings that preserve neighborhood relationships.

## Stage 5 — Real-World Applications: Unsupervised Learning in Production

- Customer segmentation: cluster purchase behavior to identify high-value, at-risk, and new users.
- Feed cluster labels into targeted marketing campaigns.
- Anomaly detection: DBSCAN marks sparse points as noise — those are your anomalies in log data or sensor streams.
- Search and recommendation: PCA or autoencoders compress item feature vectors into dense embeddings.

*Applies **deep-learning-foundations** to the decision above.*

**Observable outcome:** Search and recommendation: PCA or autoencoders compress item feature vectors into dense embeddings.

## Stage 6 — What to Learn Next

- - Supervised Learning Algorithms: Regression and Classification - Machine Learning Fundamentals - Deep Learning Architectures: CNNs, RNNs, and Transformers

*Applies **vector-embeddings-and-similarity** to the decision above.*

**Observable outcome:** - Supervised Learning Algorithms: Regression and Classification - Machine Learning Fundamentals - Deep Learning Architectures: CNNs, RNNs, and Transformers

## End-to-end outcome

Spotify's "Discover Weekly" playlist groups listeners into micro-genres like "Indie Stomp and Holler" and "Vapor Twitch" — without anyone ever labeling the data.

## Scenario context

A VAE learns to compress data into a smooth probabilistic latent space, then generate new samples by decoding random points from that space. The reparameterization trick is what makes it trainable end-to-end. Reconstruction + KL divergence loss is what makes the latent space useful.

---

Sampling from a random distribution breaks gradient flow — you can't backpropagate through a random node.

The trick: separate th…

This walkthrough focuses on **The Reparameterization Trick: Why It Enables Training**.

Before making a design choice, clarify:

- Sampling from a random distribution breaks gradient flow — you can't backpropagate through a random node.
- The trick: separate the randomness.
- $$z = \mu + \sigma \cdot arepsilon, \quad arepsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I)$$ - $ arepsilon$ is sampled from a fixed standard normal — no gradient needed here.

**Concepts in play:** api-gateway, caching, quantization-and-llm-inference, api-security-oauth2

## Stage 1 — Compress-Then-Imagine: What VAEs Actually Do

- Stability AI uses a VAE as the compression layer in Stable Diffusion — it compresses a 512×512 image to a 64×64 latent before the diffusion process, making generation 8× faster.
- Understanding VAEs means understanding why diffusion models are tractable.
- A standard autoencoder compresses input to a fixed point in latent space — like saving one GPS coordinate for each photograph.
- Generate a new image by sampling nearby?

*Applies **api-gateway** to the decision above.*

**Observable outcome:** Generate a new image by sampling nearby?

## Stage 2 — The Basics: Autoencoders and Latent Space

- To understand VAEs, start with the standard autoencoder .
- An autoencoder compresses input data into a smaller vector (the latent code), then reconstructs the original from that code.
- It learns compression and decompression jointly through backpropagation.
- The latent space is that compressed representation.

*Applies **caching** to the decision above.*

**Observable outcome:** The latent space is that compressed representation.

## Stage 3 — The Three-Block Architecture

- architecture { "version": 1, "title": "The Three-Block Architecture - Subsystem Overview", "description": "Decoupled system architecture isolating ingress, stateless logic, and persistent datastores.", "view": "high-lev…
- Sampling → draws a latent point using the reparameterization trick.
- Decoder → reconstructs the input from that latent point.

*Applies **quantization-and-llm-inference** to the decision above.*

```mermaid

```

```

flowchart LR
    A[Input x] --> B[Encoder
CNN or MLP]
    B --> C[mu and log_var
two output heads]
    C --> D[Reparameterize
z = mu + sigma  eps]
    D --> E[Decoder
CNN-T or MLP]
    E --> F[Reconstruction x_hat]
```

**Observable outcome:** Decoder → reconstructs the input from that latent point.

## Stage 4 — Deep Dive: How the VAE Latent Space Becomes Smooth

- Standard autoencoders scatter latent points arbitrarily — decoding between two known points yields noise.
- VAEs enforce smoothness by training the encoder to produce overlapping distributions rather than isolated points.
- The KL divergence term penalizes distributions that deviate from a standard normal, pulling all encoded regions toward a shared origin.
- The result: any point sampled from N(0, I) decodes into something plausible, because the entire latent space was regularized during training.

*Applies **api-security-oauth2** to the decision above.*

**Observable outcome:** The result: any point sampled from N(0, I) decodes into something plausible, because the entire latent space was regularized during training.

## Stage 5 — The Loss Function: Reconstruction + Regularization

- The VAE trains with two objectives simultaneously: $$\mathcal{L} = \underbrace{\mathbb{E}[\log p(x \mid z)]} {\text{reconstruction loss}} - \underbrace{D {KL}(q(z x) \ p(z))} {\text{KL regularization}}$$ In practice: -…
- - KL divergence = how far the encoded distribution is from a standard normal prior.

*Applies **api-gateway** to the decision above.*

```python
def vae_loss(x, x_hat, mu, log_var):
    recon_loss = torch.nn.functional.mse_loss(x_hat, x, reduction='sum')
    kl_loss    = -0.5 * torch.sum(1 + log_var - mu**2 - torch.exp(log_var))
    return recon_loss + kl_loss
```

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant I as Input
    participant E as Encoder
    participant Z as Latent z
    participant D as Decoder
    participant L as Loss
    I->>E: forward pass
    E->>Z: sample from q(z|x)
    Z->>D: decode
    D->>L: reconstruction loss
    L->>L: add KL divergence
    L-->>E: backprop gradients
```

**Observable outcome:** - KL divergence = how far the encoded distribution is from a standard normal prior.

## Stage 6 — Real-World Applications: What You Can Build with a VAE

- Image generation and interpolation: Smooth interpolation between two images — sample latent points between two encoded images and decode each.
- Quality check for latent space structure.
- Anomaly detection: Train on normal data.
- At inference, reconstruction error flags anomalies.

*Applies **caching** to the decision above.*

```python
# Anomaly detection sketch
x_hat, mu, log_var = model(x)
recon_error = ((x_hat - x) ** 2).mean(dim=1)
anomaly_flag = recon_error > THRESHOLD
```

**Observable outcome:** At inference, reconstruction error flags anomalies.

## End-to-end outcome

Sampling from a random distribution breaks gradient flow — you can't backpropagate through a random node.

record.markdownContent:
## Scenario context

A watermark tells Spark Structured Streaming: "I will accept events up to N minutes late, and then I am done waiting." Spark tracks the maximum event time seen per partition, takes the global minimum across all partitions, subtracts the threshold, and uses that as the watermark. Windows whose end time falls before the watermark are finalized and evicted from the state store. Setting the threshold too short drops rea…

This walkthrough focuses on **The Late Payment Problem: When Waiting Forever Is Not an Option**.

Before making a design choice, clarify:

- A mobile payments company processes hundreds of thousands of transactions per second.
- Their fraud detection pipeline aggregates payment events by merchant and computes rolling five-minute totals to spot unusual velocity patterns.
- The source is a Kafka topic; the sink is a Delta Lake table consumed by a risk-scoring service.

**Concepts in play:** spark-data-engineering, event-driven-architecture, core-algorithm-patterns, data-warehousing-lakehouse

## Stage 1 — Event Time, Processing Time, and What It Means for a Window to Be "Late"

- Before watermarks make sense, it is essential to understand the three different clocks that exist inside a streaming system — and why only one of them reflects what actually happened in the physical world.
- Event time is the timestamp embedded in the event itself, reflecting when the action occurred.
- For a payment, it is the moment the cardholder tapped their phone.
- This is the timestamp that matters for business logic: a fraud velocity check must use event time, not arrival time, because a genuine burst of spending looks different from a delayed batch of retransmissions.

*Applies **spark-data-engineering** to the decision above.*

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["New event arrives"] --> B{"Window type?"}
    B -- Tumbling --> C["Assign event to exactly one fixed window"]
    B -- Sliding --> D["Assign event to multiple overlapping windows"]
    B -- Session --> E["Extend existing session or open new session gap"]
    C --> F["One state entry updated"]
    D --> G["Multiple state entries updated - higher memory cost"]
    E --> H["Dynamic window boundary - variable state size"]
    F --> I["Watermark passes window end - finalize and evict"]
    G --> I
    H --> I
```

**Observable outcome:** This is the timestamp that matters for business logic: a fraud velocity check must use event time, not arrival time, because a genuine burst of spending looks different from a delayed batch of retransmissions.

## Stage 2 — How Spark Tracks the Watermark and Decides When a Window Is Safe to Close

- The watermark is not a static value.
- It advances forward as Spark observes newer event times in the data stream.
- Understanding how that advancement works — and what it controls — is the key to sizing thresholds correctly.
- The watermark formula is simple: When Spark processes each micro-batch, it scans all the event timestamps in that batch, finds the maximum, and updates its internal watermark tracker if this maximum exceeds the previous…

*Applies **event-driven-architecture** to the decision above.*

```
current watermark = max event time seen so far − late threshold
```

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Event arrives in micro-batch"] --> B["Extract event timestamp"]
    B --> C["Compute max event time in this micro-batch"]
    C --> D["Update watermark = max event time - threshold"]
    D --> E{"Is event timestamp >= watermark?"}
    E -- Yes --> F["Accept event - assign to window"]
    E -- No --> G["Drop event - too late"]
    F --> H["Update partial aggregation in state store"]
    H --> I{"Watermark now exceeds window end?"}
    I -- Yes --> J["Finalize window - emit result - evict state"]
    I -- No --> K["Window stays open in state store"]
```

**Observable outcome:** The watermark formula is simple: When Spark processes each micro-batch, it scans all the event timestamps in that batch, finds the maximum, and updates its internal watermark tracker if this maximum exceeds the previous…

## Stage 3 — Deep Dive into Watermark Internals and State Store Performance

- The Internals of Watermark Tracking Across Partitions and Micro-Batches The phrase "max event time seen so far" conceals an important distributed-systems subtlety.
- Spark does not have a single global event-time tracker.
- Each executor processes its own partition of the Kafka input stream independently.
- Events in partition 0 may be several minutes ahead of events in partition 3 if one Kafka consumer is lagging.

*Applies **core-algorithm-patterns** to the decision above.*

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    Driver["Driver Node"]
    Planner["Query Planner"]
    Optimizer["Catalyst Optimizer"]
    Executor["Executor Task"]
    
    Driver -->|"Spark Execution"| Planner
    Planner --> Optimizer
    Optimizer -->|"Optimized Plan"| Executor
    Executor -->|"Result"| Driver
```

**Observable outcome:** Events in partition 0 may be several minutes ahead of events in partition 3 if one Kafka consumer is lagging.

## Stage 4 — How Events Flow Through Watermark Tracking to Window Finalization

- The following diagram traces the complete path an event takes from Kafka partition arrival through per-partition tracking, global watermark computation, window finalization, and state eviction.
- Each step is a distinct responsibility in the Spark internals.
- Read this diagram from top to bottom: three Kafka partitions deliver events processed by three executors, each tracking its local maximum event time.
- The Driver collects these maxes and takes the global minimum (14:09 — the slowest partition sets the pace).

*Applies **data-warehousing-lakehouse** to the decision above.*

```mermaid
graph TD
    KafkaP0[Kafka Partition 0 - max event time 14:12]
    KafkaP1[Kafka Partition 1 - max event time 14:09]
    KafkaP2[Kafka Partition 2 - max event time 14:11]
    Executor0[Executor 0 - tracks local max 14:12]
    Executor1[Executor 1 - tracks local max 14:09]
    Executor2[Executor 2 - tracks local max 14:11]
    Driver[Driver - collects per-partition maxes]
    GlobalMin[Global Min = 14:09 with threshold 5 min]
    Watermark[New Watermark = 14:04]
    StateStore[State Store - scan for finalizable windows]
    FinalizeWindow[Finalize windows ending before 14:04]
    EmitResult[Emit window results in append mode]
    EvictState[Evict finalized state entries]
    DropLate[Drop late events with event time before 14:04]

    KafkaP0 --> Executor0
    KafkaP1 --> Executor1
    KafkaP2 --> Executor2
    Executor0 --> Driver
    Executor1 --> Driver
    Executor2 --> Driver
    Driver --> GlobalMin
    GlobalMin --> Watermark
    Watermark --> StateStore
    StateStore --> FinalizeWindow
    FinalizeWindow --> EmitResult
    FinalizeWindow --> EvictState
    Watermark --> DropLate
```

**Observable outcome:** The Driver collects these maxes and takes the global minimum (14:09 — the slowest partition sets the pace).

## Stage 5 — Where Watermarks Shape Real Production Streaming Pipelines

- Tumbling-window payment aggregations with withWatermark.
- The canonical use case: aggregate payment events by merchant in 5-minute tumbling windows to feed a fraud detection model.
- A 10-minute watermark threshold accommodates typical mobile network retries and brief signal loss.
- Windows are finalized 15 minutes after their start time in steady-state operation (5-minute window duration plus 10-minute threshold): a healthy trade-off between latency and completeness.

*Applies **spark-data-engineering** to the decision above.*

**Observable outcome:** Windows are finalized 15 minutes after their start time in steady-state operation (5-minute window duration plus 10-minute threshold): a healthy trade-off between latency and completeness.

## Stage 6 — Choosing Your Watermark Threshold: Latency Requirement Versus Late Data Tolerance

- Use this table as a starting point.
- Measure your actual late-event distribution from Kafka consumer lag metrics before committing to a threshold in production.
- The compliance-grade row is important: when business requirements demand both real-time output and guaranteed completeness, a single watermark threshold cannot satisfy both.
- The standard solution is a Lambda architecture: the streaming pipeline with a conservative threshold provides near-real-time results, and a nightly batch job re-processes the raw events with exact correctness to produce…

*Applies **event-driven-architecture** to the decision above.*

**Observable outcome:** The standard solution is a Lambda architecture: the streaming pipeline with a conservative threshold provides near-real-time results, and a nightly batch job re-processes the raw events with exact correctness to produce…

## End-to-end outcome

A mobile payments company processes hundreds of thousands of transactions per second.

## Alternatives considered

The source focuses on one primary design. A second architecture is not compared, so no alternative is invented here.

## Failure and degraded modes

### The Completeness-vs-Latency Tradeoff and Where Output Mode Fits In

- **Detection:** Every watermark threshold decision is a point on a single spectrum: Short threshold (1–5 minutes): - Watermark advances quickly → windows finalize sooner → state is small → output latency is low.
- **User or operator impact:** Every watermark threshold decision is a point on a single spectrum: Short threshold (1–5 minutes): - Watermark advances quickly → windows finalize sooner → state is small → output latency is low.

record.markdownContent:
## Scenario context

Webhooks let one system push event data to another the moment something happens. Instead of polling ("anything new?"), you expose an endpoint and the provider POSTs signed event payloads to you in near real-time. The key production requirements: signature verification, idempotency, async processing.

---

Webhook providers guarantee delivery by retrying on failure — not by ensuring exactly-once. A network timeout af…

This walkthrough focuses on **Deep Dive: Why At-Least-Once Delivery Demands Idempotency**.

Before making a design choice, clarify:

- Webhook providers guarantee delivery by retrying on failure — not by ensuring exactly-once.
- A network timeout after your handler processes an event but before returning 200 causes the same event to arrive again.
- Idempotency means processing an event twice produces the same result as once.

**Concepts in play:** api-gateway, event-driven-architecture, stack-and-queue-data-structures, circuit-breaker

## Stage 1 — The Basics: HTTP Callbacks and Event-Driven Delivery

- A webhook is an HTTP callback.
- When a specific event occurs, the event source (provider) sends an HTTP POST request to a URL you specify — your webhook endpoint.
- No polling, no long connections.
- The three-step registration flow: 1.

*Applies **api-gateway** to the decision above.*

**Observable outcome:** The three-step registration flow: 1.

## Stage 2 — Stop Polling — Let the Provider Ring Your Doorbell

- Polling means your app repeatedly asks a provider "anything new?" — burning bandwidth and adding latency whether or not anything changed.
- Webhooks invert the call: you register a URL, and the provider calls your endpoint the instant an event occurs.
- Analogy: Polling is calling the courier every 5 minutes.
- A webhook is the courier ringing your doorbell the moment the package arrives.

*Applies **event-driven-architecture** to the decision above.*

**Observable outcome:** A webhook is the courier ringing your doorbell the moment the package arrives.

## Stage 3 — What a Webhook Payload Looks Like

- Most providers send a structured JSON body over HTTPS POST: Key fields in every real-world webhook: - id — unique event identifier; use for deduplication.
- - type — event name; drives routing in your handler.
- - created — Unix timestamp; enables replay-window validation.
- - data — the event payload; schema varies by event type.

*Applies **stack-and-queue-data-structures** to the decision above.*

```json
{
  "id":      "evt_101",
  "type":    "payment.succeeded",
  "created": 1772877602,
  "data": {
    "transaction_id": "txn_9001",
    "amount":         4999,
    "currency":       "USD"
  }
}
```

**Observable outcome:** - data — the event payload; schema varies by event type.

## Stage 4 — Webhook Delivery Flow

- The complete lifecycle from event to processed business logic: The critical design principle: your endpoint's only job is to acknowledge receipt (return 200) as fast as possible.
- All actual work happens asynchronously.
- This prevents provider retry storms.
- Provider retry schedules (common defaults): Providers consider a delivery successful only when they receive a 2xx response within their timeout window (usually 5–30 seconds).

*Applies **circuit-breaker** to the decision above.*

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Event occurs at Provider] --> B[Provider signs payload with HMAC]
    B --> C[Provider POSTs to your endpoint over HTTPS]
    C --> D{Signature valid?}
    D -->|No| E[Return 401  reject]
    D -->|Yes| F{Event ID already seen?}
    F -->|Yes| G[Return 200  silently ignore]
    F -->|No| H[Persist raw payload to DB]
    H --> I[Enqueue job for async worker]
    I --> J[Return 200 immediately]
    J --> K[Worker executes business logic]
    K --> L[Mark event as processed]
```

**Observable outcome:** Provider retry schedules (common defaults): Providers consider a delivery successful only when they receive a 2xx response within their timeout window (usually 5–30 seconds).

## Stage 5 — The Production-Safe Webhook Handler

- A naive endpoint that just processes inline is dangerous: it creates duplicate actions when providers retry.
- The correct pattern has 5 ordered steps: Why return 200 before processing?
- Most providers retry if they don't receive a timely 2xx.
- If your business logic runs inline and takes too long, the same event fires twice.

*Applies **api-gateway** to the decision above.*

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Provider POST] --> B{Valid HMAC
signature?}
    B -->|No| C[Return 401]
    B -->|Yes| D{Duplicate
event_id?}
    D -->|Yes| E[Return 200  ignore]
    D -->|No| F[Persist event
to durable store]
    F --> G[Enqueue for async
worker]
    G --> H[Return 200 immediately]
    H --> I[Worker processes
business logic]
```

```javascript
// Node.js / Express — production-safe handler skeleton
app.post('/webhooks/provider', express.raw({ type: 'application/json' }), (req, res) => {
  const sig = req.header('X-Signature');
  if (!isValidHmac(req.body, sig, process.env.WEBHOOK_SECRET)) {
    return res.status(401).send('invalid signature');
  }

  const event = JSON.parse(req.body.toString('utf8'));

  if (isDuplicate(event.id)) {
    return res.status(200).send('duplicate ignored');
  }

  persistEvent(event);    // write to DB before ack
  enqueueEvent(event);    // hand off to async worker
  return res.status(200).send('accepted');
});
```

**Observable outcome:** If your business logic runs inline and takes too long, the same event fires twice.

## Stage 6 — Real-World Applications: Where Webhooks Power Real Systems

- 

*Applies **event-driven-architecture** to the decision above.*

**Observable outcome:** You can explain how “Real-World Applications: Where Webhooks Power Real Systems” changes the architecture or implementation path.

## End-to-end outcome

Webhook providers guarantee delivery by retrying on failure — not by ensuring exactly-once.

## Alternatives considered

### Decision Guide: When Webhooks Are (and Aren't) the Answer

### Trade-offs & Failure Modes: Failure Modes You Must Defend Against

- **Detection:** Most webhook providers use at-least-once delivery — duplicates are normal, ordering is not guaranteed.
- **User or operator impact:** Most webhook providers use at-least-once delivery — duplicates are normal, ordering is not guaranteed.

record.markdownContent:
## Scenario context

A hash table gives you near-O(1) lookups, inserts, and deletes by using a **hash function** to map keys to array indices. The tradeoff: collisions (when two keys hash to the same slot) must be handled, and a full hash table must be resized.

---

Python `dict` uses open addressing with **compact arrays** (since Python 3.6). Entries are stored in an incrementally-growing compact array indexed by insertion order, with…

This walkthrough focuses on **Why Python Dicts Are Fast**.

Before making a design choice, clarify:

- Python dict uses open addressing with compact arrays (since Python 3.6).
- Entries are stored in an incrementally-growing compact array indexed by insertion order, with a separate hash table of indices pointing into it.
- This gives: - Fast iteration (compact memory, no pointer chasing).

**Concepts in play:** hash-tables-and-bloom-filters, database-indexing, api-gateway, jvm-internals-and-garbage-collection

## Stage 1 — The Magic Mailroom Stamp

- Imagine a mailroom with 100 drawers.
- A magic stamp converts any employee name to a number 1–100.
- Stamp "John" → you get 42 → open Drawer 42.
- That stamp is a hash function .

*Applies **hash-tables-and-bloom-filters** to the decision above.*

**Observable outcome:** That stamp is a hash function .

## Stage 2 — Hash Table Fundamentals

- A hash table combines two simple ideas into a data structure with near-constant-time performance: 1.
- An array provides O(1) access by index: array[42] is instant.
- A hash function converts any key (string, integer, object) to an index: h("john") → 42 .
- Together: given any key, compute its index in one step, then access the array slot directly.

*Applies **database-indexing** to the decision above.*

**Observable outcome:** Together: given any key, compute its index in one step, then access the array slot directly.

## Stage 3 — Deep Dive: Array + Hash Function

- Deterministic: Same input always produces the same output.
- Uniform: Keys distribute evenly to minimize collisions.
- Simple hash function (NOT production-quality): Python's built-in hash() uses SipHash (cryptographically secure version) to prevent hash flooding attacks.

*Applies **api-gateway** to the decision above.*

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    Key[Key: 'cat'] --> HashFn["Hash Function h('cat') = 2"]
    HashFn --> Array[Array [0][1][2: 'catmeow'][3]...]
    Array --> Value[Value: 'meow']
```

```python
def simple_hash(key: str, size: int) -> int:
    return sum(ord(c) for c in key) % size
```

**Observable outcome:** Simple hash function (NOT production-quality): Python's built-in hash() uses SipHash (cryptographically secure version) to prevent hash flooding attacks.

## Stage 4 — How a Hash Table Handles a Lookup

- The lookup flow for key "alice" in a hash table with separate chaining: Three scenarios during lookup: 1.
- Direct hit: array[index] contains exactly the target key → O(1).
- Collision chain: array[index] has multiple entries → scan the short chain → O(k) where k = bucket length (typically 1–2 with good load factor).
- Miss: The slot is empty → key not in table → O(1).

*Applies **jvm-internals-and-garbage-collection** to the decision above.*

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    K[Key: 'alice'] --> HF["Hash Function: h('alice') = 7"]
    HF --> IDX[Array index 7]
    IDX --> BK[Bucket 7: [('alice', 25), ('charlie', 30)]]
    BK --> SCAN{Scan bucket: key == 'alice'?}
    SCAN -->|Match found| RET[Return value: 25]
    SCAN -->|No match| MISS[Return None / KeyError]
    style RET fill:#90EE90
    style MISS fill:#FFB6C1
```

**Observable outcome:** Miss: The slot is empty → key not in table → O(1).

## Stage 5 — Collisions: When Two Keys Land in the Same Slot

- Given a finite array, two different keys will eventually map to the same slot.
- Example: - hash('cat') = 2 → Stored at index 2.
- - hash('bird') = 2 → Collision at index 2!
- Two collision resolution strategies: Separate Chaining Each slot holds a linked list of key-value pairs.

*Applies **hash-tables-and-bloom-filters** to the decision above.*

```
index 2: [('cat', 'meow') → ('bird', 'tweet')]
```

```
hash('cat') = 2 → store at 2
hash('bird') = 2 (full) → probe 3 → store at 3
```

**Observable outcome:** Two collision resolution strategies: Separate Chaining Each slot holds a linked list of key-value pairs.

## Stage 6 — Deep Dive: Load Factor and Rehashing

- Load factor = (number of entries) / (array capacity).
- As the table fills up (load factor → 1.0), collisions increase and performance degrades.
- Standard practice: rehash when load factor exceeds 0.75 .
- Create a new array 2× the size.

*Applies **database-indexing** to the decision above.*

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Insert new key] --> B{Load factor > 0.75?}
    B -- No --> C[Insert into current array]
    C --> D["O(1) average"]
    B -- Yes --> E[Allocate 2x array]
    E --> F[Re-hash all existing keys]
    F --> G[Insert new key]
    G --> H[Old array GC'd]
    H --> I["Amortized O(1) per insert"]
```

**Observable outcome:** Create a new array 2× the size.

## End-to-end outcome

Python dict uses open addressing with compact arrays (since Python 3.6).

## Alternatives considered

The source focuses on one primary design. A second architecture is not compared, so no alternative is invented here.

## Failure and degraded modes

### Trade-offs & Failure Modes: Trade-offs, Failure Modes & Decision Guide: Hash Tables vs Others

- **Detection:** Choose hash table when: You need fast key-value lookup and don't need ordering or range queries.
- **User or operator impact:** Choose hash table when: You need fast key-value lookup and don't need ordering or range queries.

### What Hash Tables Teach You About Trade-offs

- **Detection:** - O(1) average is not O(1) guaranteed.
- **User or operator impact:** - O(1) average is not O(1) guaranteed.

## Scenario context

Logits are the raw, unnormalized scores produced by the final layer of a neural network — before any probability transformation. Softmax converts them to probabilities. Temperature scales them before Softmax to control output randomness.

---

1. **Training stability:** Working with logits and applying log-Softmax is numerically more stable than computing probabilities first, then taking their logarithm for the **cr…

This walkthrough focuses on **Why Not Output Probabilities Directly?**.

Before making a design choice, clarify:

- Training stability: Working with logits and applying log-Softmax is numerically more stable than computing probabilities first, then taking their logarithm for the cross-entropy loss — the standard training objective th…
- Flexibility: The same logits can be processed differently (Softmax for classification, sigmoid for multi-label, raw for regression).
- Temperature scaling: You can reshape the distribution from the logits before applying Softmax, which you couldn't do if the network directly output probabilities.

**Concepts in play:** vector-embeddings-and-similarity, llm-prompt-engineering, deep-learning-foundations, quantization-and-llm-inference

## Stage 1 — The Confidence Meter Before Calibration

- A doctor looks at an X-ray and assigns a raw "gut score": Cancer likelihood = 8.2, Normal = 1.4.
- These numbers are not percentages — they haven't been normalized yet.
- To get percentages, she runs them through a calibration formula.
- Logits are those raw gut scores.

*Applies **vector-embeddings-and-similarity** to the decision above.*

**Observable outcome:** Logits are those raw gut scores.

## Stage 2 — What Exactly Is a Logit?

- The word logit comes from statistics — it's short for "log-odds unit." In modern deep learning, the term is used more loosely to mean the raw, unnormalized score produced by the final linear layer of a neural network be…
- Think of a neural network as a pipeline: raw inputs pass through multiple layers of transformations, and at the very end, a linear layer projects everything into a vector of numbers — one number per possible output clas…
- Key properties of logits: - They can be any real number — positive, negative, or zero.
- - A higher logit means the network is more confident in that class relative to others.

*Applies **llm-prompt-engineering** to the decision above.*

**Observable outcome:** - A higher logit means the network is more confident in that class relative to others.

## Stage 3 — From Network Output to Prediction

- A classification network predicting image labels outputs raw scores: These numbers have no fixed scale.
- A "4.5" just means "more confident Cat than the others." Softmax converts logits to probabilities: $$P i = \frac{e^{z i}}{\sum j e^{z j}}$$ Applied to the example — computing e^4.5 = 90.02, e^−1.2 = 0.30, e^0.8 = 2.23,…
- 📊 Logits to Token Pipeline This flowchart traces the journey of a raw logit vector from model output to a sampled output token.
- Starting with the raw scores produced by the final linear layer, Softmax converts them into a probability distribution, Top-K filtering narrows the candidates to the most likely tokens, and sampling draws the final outp…

*Applies **deep-learning-foundations** to the decision above.*

```
Raw output (logits):
  Cat:  4.5
  Dog: -1.2
  Bird: 0.8
```

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    LG[Raw Logits] --> SM[Softmax]
    SM --> PR[Probabilities]
    PR --> TK[Top-K Filter]
    TK --> SP[Sample Token]
    SP --> OUT[Output Token]
```

**Observable outcome:** Starting with the raw scores produced by the final linear layer, Softmax converts them into a probability distribution, Top-K filtering narrows the candidates to the most likely tokens, and sampling draws the final outp…

## Stage 4 — The Logit Pipeline: From Input to Prediction

- Here is how logits flow through the full inference pipeline in a classification or language model: Step-by-step: 1.
- Input — raw data (tokens, pixels) enters the network.
- Hidden layers — extract abstract features through multiple transformations.
- Linear layer — maps features to a logit per class (no activation, just weights × input + bias).

*Applies **quantization-and-llm-inference** to the decision above.*

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    Input["Input Data (text, image, etc.)"] --> Encoder["Encoder / Hidden Layers (feature extraction)"]
    Encoder --> Linear["Final Linear Layer (produces raw logits z_i)"]
    Linear --> Temp[" Temperature T (optional scaling)"]
    Temp --> Softmax[Softmax  probability distribution P_i]
    Softmax --> Decision[Argmax or Sampling  predicted class / next token]
```

**Observable outcome:** Linear layer — maps features to a logit per class (no activation, just weights × input + bias).

## Stage 5 — Deep Dive: Temperature: Reshaping the Logit Distribution

- In language models, the vocabulary logits are scaled by a temperature $T$ before Softmax: $$P i = \frac{\exp(z i / T)}{\sum j \exp(z j / T)}$$ Effect of temperature on the cat/dog/bird example (logits: 4.5, -1.2, 0.8):…
- Repetitive in language models.

*Applies **vector-embeddings-and-similarity** to the decision above.*

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    Hidden[Hidden Layer Output] --> Logits["Logit Layer (raw z_i scores)"]
    Logits --> Temp[ Temperature T]
    Temp --> Softmax[Softmax  probabilities P_i]
    Softmax --> Sample[Sample or Argmax  predicted class / next token]
```

**Observable outcome:** Repetitive in language models.

## Stage 6 — Real-World Applications of Logits

- Logits appear in almost every modern ML system.
- Here are concrete examples of where they matter: 1.
- Large Language Models (ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude) Every time an LLM generates the next word, it produces a logit for every token in its vocabulary (often 50,000+ tokens).
- Temperature and top-k/top-p sampling are applied to these logits before selecting the next token.

*Applies **llm-prompt-engineering** to the decision above.*

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Context Tokens
    participant M as LLM
    participant L as Logits
    participant S as Sampler
    C->>M: input sequence
    M->>L: compute logits
    L->>S: apply temperature
    S-->>C: append new token
    C->>M: next iteration
```

**Observable outcome:** Temperature and top-k/top-p sampling are applied to these logits before selecting the next token.

## End-to-end outcome

Training stability: Working with logits and applying log-Softmax is numerically more stable than computing probabilities first, then taking their logarithm for the cross-entropy loss — the standard training objective that penalizes the model proportionally to how wrong its predicted probability distribution is compared to the true label.

alternatives.title: Every database scaling journey begins with a single server running a database engine like PostgreSQL or MySQL. In the early stages, this setup is simple and robust. However, as the application gains traction, read and write traffic increases, and the database file size grows. Eventually, the server will saturate its hardware limits (CPU, Memory, Disk I/O).
alternatives.explanation: At this stage, architects face a choice between two scaling vectors:

alternatives.title: 1. Vertical Scaling (Scale Up)
alternatives.explanation: Vertical scaling involves adding more power to the existing server: upgrading to faster CPUs, installing more RAM, or moving to higher-throughput NVMe SSD storage arrays.

alternatives.title: 2. Horizontal Scaling (Scale Out)
alternatives.explanation: Horizontal scaling involves distributing the database workload across multiple independent database servers (nodes).

alternatives.title: It is critical to distinguish between database partitioning and database sharding. While they both divide a large dataset into smaller subsets, they operate at different architectural boundaries.
alternatives.explanation: It is critical to distinguish between database partitioning and database sharding. While they both divide a large dataset into smaller subsets, they operate at different architectural boundaries.

alternatives.title: Database Partitioning
alternatives.explanation: Database partitioning divides a single large table into smaller, more manageable physical subsets (partitions) within the same database server .

alternatives.title: Database Sharding
alternatives.explanation: Database sharding goes a step further: it distributes those table partitions across completely separate physical database instances running on different servers .

alternatives.title: Decision Guide: Selecting the Sharding Strategy
alternatives.explanation: Use this matrix to select the sharding strategy for your workload: - Use Algorithmic (Hash-Based) Sharding if: - Your read/write workload is distributed randomly and you need to prevent hot spots.

failuresAndDegradedModes.behavior: Sharding is an architectural last resort. While it solves scaling limits, it introduces severe design challenges:

failuresAndDegradedModes.name: 1. Cross-Shard Joins
failuresAndDegradedModes.behavior: You cannot execute a standard SQL JOIN query across tables located on different physical shards.

failuresAndDegradedModes.name: 2. Distributed Transactions (Two-Phase Commit)
failuresAndDegradedModes.behavior: Maintaining ACID properties across multiple database nodes requires a Distributed Transaction Coordinator and protocols like Two-Phase Commit (2PC) .

failuresAndDegradedModes.name: 3. Distributed ID Generation
failuresAndDegradedModes.behavior: In a single-node database, you can rely on auto-incrementing integer primary keys.

## Scenario context

When a database outgrows a single server's capacity, horizontal scaling becomes necessary. **Partitioning** splits tables locally within a single database instance, while **Sharding** distributes data across completely separate physical database servers. Sharding keys determine how records are routed, utilizing hash-based, range-based, or lookup-based strategies.



```architecture
{
  "version": 1,
  "title": "TLDR…

This walkthrough focuses on **The Scaling Problem: Up vs. Out**.

Before making a design choice, clarify:

- Every database scaling journey begins with a single server running a database engine like PostgreSQL or MySQL.
- In the early stages, this setup is simple and robust.
- However, as the application gains traction, read and write traffic increases, and the database file size grows.

**Concepts in play:** database-sharding, caching, consistency-replication, jvm-internals-and-garbage-collection

## Stage 1 — Sharding Strategies

- To implement sharding, you must choose a Sharding Key —the column(s) in your table used to determine which shard a record belongs to.
- Choosing the correct sharding key is the most critical decision in distributed database design.
- Algorithmic (Hash-Based) Sharding In hash-based sharding, the load is distributed by applying a hash function to the sharding key, followed by a modulo operation: $$\text{Shard ID} = \text{Hash}(\text{Sharding Key}) \pm…
- - Cons: - Re-sharding Complexity: If you add a new shard, the modulo denominator changes.

*Applies **database-sharding** to the decision above.*

```architecture
{
  "version": 1,
  "title": "Sharding Strategies - Storage Topology",
  "description": "Multi-tier caching and replicated storage pipeline ensuring fast reads and transactional consistency.",
  "view": "data-flow",
  "pattern": "cache-aside",
  "direction": "LR",
  "groups": [
    { "id": "compute", "label": "Application Workers", "tone": "blue" },
    { "id": "cache-tier", "label": "Volatile Memory Tier", "tone": "amber" },
    { "id": "storage-tier", "label": "Persistent Disk Tier", "tone": "green" }
  ],
  "nodes": [
    { "id": "worker", "component": "workflow-service", "label": "Worker Process", "group": "compute" },
    { "id": "mem", "component": "redis", "label": "In-Memory Cache", "group": "cache-tier", "badge": "Hot Keys" },
    { "id": "primary", "component": "postgres", "label": "Primary Database", "group": "storage-tier", "badge": "Write Master" }
  ],
  "edges": [
    { "from": "worker", "to": "mem", "kind": "read", "label": "Fast Read" },
    { "from": "worker", "to": "primary", "kind": "write", "label": "Transactional Commit" }
  ],
  "takeaway": {
    "title": "Storage Access Pattern",
    "body": "In-memory caching handles high-frequency read spikes, reserving disk transactions strictly for state modifications."
  }

```

**Observable outcome:** - Cons: - Re-sharding Complexity: If you add a new shard, the modulo denominator changes.

## Stage 2 — Deep Dive: Consistent Hashing and the Hash Ring

- To solve the re-sharding limitation of algorithmic sharding (where adding a node requires migrating almost all data), architects use Consistent Hashing .
- Consistent hashing maps both the database shards and the sharding keys onto a logical circular space called a Hash Ring (typically from $0$ to $2^{32} - 1$).
- Mapping Nodes: Each database shard is hashed based on its IP or hostname, and placed at a coordinate on the ring.
- Mapping Keys: When a record is inserted, its sharding key is hashed and mapped to a coordinate on the ring.

*Applies **caching** to the decision above.*

```
            Shard A (Hash: 1000)
             /                \
   Key 1 (Hash: 200)           Key 2 (Hash: 1500)
           /                    \
  Shard C (Hash: 3000) ------- Shard B (Hash: 2000)
```

**Observable outcome:** Mapping Keys: When a record is inserted, its sharding key is hashed and mapped to a coordinate on the ring.

## Stage 3 — Partitioning Inside One Database

- Partitioning divides one logical table into physical pieces managed by the same database.
- Horizontal partitioning splits rows; vertical partitioning separates groups of columns, often moving large or rarely accessed fields away from the hot row.
- PostgreSQL supports range, list, and hash partitions while preserving one SQL-facing table.
- ~~~sql CREATE TABLE orders ( id bigint NOT NULL, tenant id bigint NOT NULL, created at timestamptz NOT NULL, total cents bigint NOT NULL ) PARTITION BY RANGE (created at); CREATE TABLE orders 2026 07 PARTITION OF orders…

*Applies **consistency-replication** to the decision above.*

## Stage 4 — Choosing a Shard Key

- A useful shard key has high cardinality, stable ownership, even traffic distribution, and alignment with common queries.
- Evaluate data volume and request rate separately: ten equally sized tenants are not balanced if one produces 80% of traffic.
- Before committing, replay a representative query log against the proposed key.

*Applies **jvm-internals-and-garbage-collection** to the decision above.*

## Stage 5 — Online Resharding Without a Long Outage

- Resharding is a migration, not a configuration toggle: 1.
- Create the destination shard and a versioned shard map.
- Snapshot-copy the selected key range while normal writes continue.
- Capture concurrent changes through CDC or an outbox.

*Applies **database-sharding** to the decision above.*

## Stage 6 — Cross-Shard Operations

- Global uniqueness can use a globally unique ID generator, a dedicated registry, or IDs scoped by shard.
- Cross-shard pagination needs a cursor per shard plus a merge step; an offset applied independently to every shard is neither efficient nor stable.
- Aggregations should usually flow into a separate analytical store rather than fan out across every transactional shard on each request.
- For financial workflows, prefer keeping one invariant inside one shard.

*Applies **caching** to the decision above.*

**Observable outcome:** For financial workflows, prefer keeping one invariant inside one shard.

## End-to-end outcome

After working through the stages, you should be able to explain:

- - Partitioning improves manageability inside one database; sharding distributes ownership across databases.
- - A shard key is an operational commitment encoded in every important query.

## Alternatives considered

### Every database scaling journey begins with a single server running a database engine like PostgreSQL or MySQL. In the early stages, this setup is simple and robust. However, as the application gains traction, read and write traffic increases, and the database file size grows. Eventually, the server will saturate its hardware limits (CPU, Memory, Disk I/O).

At this stage, architects face a choice between two scaling vectors:

### 1. Vertical Scaling (Scale Up)

Vertical scaling involves adding more power to the existing server: upgrading to faster CPUs, installing more RAM, or moving to higher-throughput NVMe SSD storage arrays.

### 2. Horizontal Scaling (Scale Out)

Horizontal scaling involves distributing the database workload across multiple independent database servers (nodes).

### It is critical to distinguish between database partitioning and database sharding. While they both divide a large dataset into smaller subsets, they operate at different architectural boundaries.

It is critical to distinguish between database partitioning and database sharding. While they both divide a large dataset into smaller subsets, they operate at different architectural boundaries.

### Database Partitioning

Database partitioning divides a single large table into smaller, more manageable physical subsets (partitions) within the same database server .

### Database Sharding

Database sharding goes a step further: it distributes those table partitions across completely separate physical database instances running on different servers .

### Decision Guide: Selecting the Sharding Strategy

Use this matrix to select the sharding strategy for your workload: - Use Algorithmic (Hash-Based) Sharding if: - Your read/write workload is distributed randomly and you need to prevent hot spots.


## Failure and degraded modes

### Sharding is an architectural last resort. While it solves scaling limits, it introduces severe design challenges:

- **Detection:** Sharding is an architectural last resort. While it solves scaling limits, it introduces severe design challenges:
- **User or operator impact:** Sharding is an architectural last resort. While it solves scaling limits, it introduces severe design challenges:

### 1. Cross-Shard Joins

- **Detection:** You cannot execute a standard SQL JOIN query across tables located on different physical shards.
- **User or operator impact:** You cannot execute a standard SQL JOIN query across tables located on different physical shards.

### 2. Distributed Transactions (Two-Phase Commit)

- **Detection:** Maintaining ACID properties across multiple database nodes requires a Distributed Transaction Coordinator and protocols like Two-Phase Commit (2PC) .
- **User or operator impact:** Maintaining ACID properties across multiple database nodes requires a Distributed Transaction Coordinator and protocols like Two-Phase Commit (2PC) .

### 3. Distributed ID Generation

- **Detection:** In a single-node database, you can rely on auto-incrementing integer primary keys.
- **User or operator impact:** In a single-node database, you can rely on auto-incrementing integer primary keys.

### Trade-offs: When to Shard

record.markdownContent:
## Scenario context

Embeddings convert words (and images, users, products) into dense numerical vectors in a geometric space where **semantic similarity = geometric proximity**. "King - Man + Woman ≈ Queen" is not magic — it is the arithmetic property of well-trained embeddings.

---

Before embeddings, machines represented words as one-hot vectors:

```
Vocabulary: [cat, dog, fish, car, truck]
"cat"  = [1, 0, 0, 0, 0]
"dog"  = [0, 1,…

This walkthrough focuses on **The One-Hot Problem: Numbers That Know Nothing**.

Before making a design choice, clarify:

- Before embeddings, machines represented words as one-hot vectors: Problems: 1.
- Sparse: 50,000-word vocab = 50,000-dimensional vectors that are 99.998% zeros.
- No similarity: The machine sees cat and dog as equally distant as cat and car .

**Concepts in play:** vector-embeddings-and-similarity, sorting-and-searching-algorithms, deep-learning-foundations, vector-databases-rag

## Stage 1 — Vectors, Dimensions, and the Geometry of Meaning

- Think of a vector as a list of numbers that acts like a GPS coordinate — except instead of latitude and longitude, it has hundreds of coordinates in "meaning space." Each number encodes some abstract feature of a word (…
- An embedding model is a neural network trained to produce these vectors.
- You feed in a word, sentence, or image, and the model outputs a dense vector — a numerical fingerprint of that input's meaning.
- Popular options include: How cosine similarity works (no math degree required): Cosine similarity measures the angle between two vectors, not the raw distance between their endpoints.

*Applies **vector-embeddings-and-similarity** to the decision above.*

```
cosine_similarity("cat",  "kitten")   ≈ 0.92   → nearly identical meaning
cosine_similarity("cat",  "dog")      ≈ 0.76   → related concepts
cosine_similarity("cat",  "database") ≈ 0.05   → unrelated
```

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    TX[Text Input] --> EM[Embedding Model]
    EM --> VEC[Vector Representation]
    VEC --> VS[Vector Space]
    VS --> CD[Cosine Distance]
    CD --> SD[Similar Documents]
```

**Observable outcome:** Popular options include: How cosine similarity works (no math degree required): Cosine similarity measures the angle between two vectors, not the raw distance between their endpoints.

## Stage 2 — Dense Vectors: Coordinates in Meaning Space

- An embedding represents a word as a dense low-dimensional vector (e.g., 300 dimensions): Cosine similarity between cat and dog: ~0.92 (very close).
- Cosine similarity between cat and car: ~0.1 (far apart).
- The model has learned that cats and dogs live in the same region of the 300D semantic space.

*Applies **sorting-and-searching-algorithms** to the decision above.*

```
"cat"  → [0.8, -0.3,  0.6, 0.1, ...]   (300 values, all non-zero)
"dog"  → [0.7, -0.2,  0.5, 0.2, ...]   (similar to cat)
"car"  → [-0.1, 0.9, -0.4, 0.8, ...]   (different region of space)
```

**Observable outcome:** The model has learned that cats and dogs live in the same region of the 300D semantic space.

## Stage 3 — The Learning Principle: "You Shall Know a Word by the Company It Keeps"

- This is Firth's distributional hypothesis (1957), and it is the foundation of word2vec, GloVe, and modern LLM embeddings.
- Training signal: Predict surrounding words.
- Words that appear in similar contexts get similar representations.
- Cat and dog both appear near "pet," "feed," "vet," "collar" → their vectors converge in the training process.

*Applies **deep-learning-foundations** to the decision above.*

```
Context window: "... feeds the ___ every morning ..."
Target word: "cat"
```

**Observable outcome:** Cat and dog both appear near "pet," "feed," "vet," "collar" → their vectors converge in the training process.

## Stage 4 — Embeddings in Production: Not Just Words

- Modern embeddings go far beyond words: Vector databases (Pinecone, Weaviate, Milvus, pgvector) store billions of embedding vectors and support approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) search — the "find the most semantically…

*Applies **vector-databases-rag** to the decision above.*

**Observable outcome:** Modern embeddings go far beyond words: Vector databases (Pinecone, Weaviate, Milvus, pgvector) store billions of embedding vectors and support approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) search — the "find the most semantically…

## Stage 5 — From Raw Text to a Point in Space: The Embedding Pipeline

- When you type a query into a semantic search engine, here is what happens under the hood — from your raw text to a meaningful coordinate in vector space: What each step does: 1.
- Tokenizer — breaks text into sub-word units.
- "sleeping" might become ["sleep", " ing"] in BERT's vocabulary, so even unknown words are represented.
- Token IDs — each token maps to an integer that the model's lookup table recognises.

*Applies **vector-embeddings-and-similarity** to the decision above.*

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[ Raw Text 'How do cats sleep?'] --> B[ Tokenizer Split into sub-word tokens]
    B --> C[ Token IDs Map each token to an integer index [2129, 103, 8855, 3581, 30]]
    C --> D[" Embedding Model Neural network forward pass (attention + feed-forward layers)"]
    D --> E[ Dense Vector [0.23, -0.41, 0.87, ..., 0.12] (e.g., 1536 dimensions)]
    E --> F[ Vector Space A point in high-dimensional semantic space]
    F --> G[ Nearest Neighbor Search Find closest vectors  retrieve similar content]
```

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant Q as Query Text
    participant M as Embed Model
    participant V as Vector DB
    participant R as Results
    Q->>M: encode query
    M->>V: 1536-dim vector
    V->>R: ANN search
    R-->>Q: top similar results
```

**Observable outcome:** Token IDs — each token maps to an integer that the model's lookup table recognises.

## Stage 6 — Real-World Applications: Embeddings Powering the Apps You Use Every Day

- Embeddings are the invisible infrastructure behind a surprising number of modern products.
- Semantic Search Google, Notion, and GitHub Copilot all use embedding-based search.
- When you type "how do I handle an exception in Python," a keyword search might miss a result titled "Python error handling best practices" because the exact words differ.
- An embedding search finds it because both phrases map to nearby vectors.

*Applies **sorting-and-searching-algorithms** to the decision above.*

**Observable outcome:** An embedding search finds it because both phrases map to nearby vectors.

## End-to-end outcome

Before embeddings, machines represented words as one-hot vectors: Problems: 1.

## Alternatives considered

### Decision Guide: Choosing the Right Embedding Approach

Use pre-trained embeddings (OpenAI, sentence-transformers) for most NLP tasks — they require no training data and perform well out of the box.


## Failure and degraded modes

### Trade-offs & Failure Modes: One-Hot vs. Dense Embeddings: The Full Picture

record.markdownContent:
## Scenario context

Write skew is the hardest concurrency anomaly to reason about: two concurrent transactions each read a shared condition, decide they can safely proceed, and then write to *different* rows. No individual operation is wrong. No row was overwritten. Yet together, their writes violate the invariant both checked. Repeatable Read does not prevent write skew — only Serializable isolation (or explicit predicate locking) can…

This walkthrough focuses on **Why Snapshot Isolation and Repeatable Read Are Not Enough**.

Before making a design choice, clarify:

- Snapshot Isolation is widely praised — and for good reason.
- It eliminates dirty reads, non-repeatable reads, and phantom reads in a single stroke by giving every transaction a consistent point-in-time view of the database.
- It does this without locking read rows, which gives it excellent throughput characteristics.

**Concepts in play:** database-isolation-levels-anomalies, caching, consistency-replication, rate-limiting

## Stage 1 — The On-Call Disaster: When Two Correct Decisions Leave Zero Doctors Available

- The hospital enforces a simple invariant: at all times, at least one doctor must have status = 'active' in the on call table.
- The rule is checked by application logic before any doctor is allowed to go off-call.
- Here is the timeline that breaks everything: - 14:00:00 — Alice opens the staff portal and clicks "Go Off Call." - 14:00:00 — Bob, in a separate browser tab, clicks "Go Off Call" simultaneously.
- - 14:00:01 — Alice's transaction reads: SELECT COUNT( ) FROM on call WHERE status = 'active' → returns 2 (Alice and Bob are both active).

*Applies **database-isolation-levels-anomalies** to the decision above.*

**Observable outcome:** - 14:00:01 — Alice's transaction reads: SELECT COUNT( ) FROM on call WHERE status = 'active' → returns 2 (Alice and Bob are both active).

## Stage 2 — What Makes Write Skew Different from Lost Updates and Dirty Reads

- Before going deeper, it is worth pinning down exactly why write skew is its own category — distinct from every other anomaly you may already know.
- Write skew is uniquely dangerous because: 1.
- Both writes succeed and survive.
- The data is not corrupted in any conventional sense — both the alice row and the bob row correctly reflect their owners' actions.

*Applies **caching** to the decision above.*

**Observable outcome:** The data is not corrupted in any conventional sense — both the alice row and the bob row correctly reflect their owners' actions.

## Stage 3 — Step-by-Step: How Two Transactions Jointly Break a Shared Invariant

- The sequence diagram below traces the exact interleaving that produces write skew.
- Both transactions are running under Snapshot Isolation (the default in PostgreSQL's REPEATABLE READ and many "snapshot" modes) — each sees a perfectly consistent point-in-time view of the database, which is precisely wh…
- Read the diagram from top to bottom.
- Both transactions start by reading the full active count from the same snapshot — both see 2.

*Applies **consistency-replication** to the decision above.*

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant T1 as T1 - Alice
    participant DB as on_call table
    participant T2 as T2 - Bob

    T1->>DB: BEGIN; SELECT COUNT(*) WHERE status=active
    DB-->>T1: 2 (alice=active, bob=active)
    T2->>DB: BEGIN; SELECT COUNT(*) WHERE status=active
    DB-->>T2: 2 (alice=active, bob=active)
    Note over T1: count=2 > 1, safe to go off call
    Note over T2: count=2 > 1, safe to go off call
    T1->>DB: UPDATE on_call SET status=off_call WHERE doctor=alice
    T2->>DB: UPDATE on_call SET status=off_call WHERE doctor=bob
    T1->>DB: COMMIT
    T2->>DB: COMMIT
    Note over DB: 0 active doctors. Invariant violated.
```

**Observable outcome:** Both transactions start by reading the full active count from the same snapshot — both see 2.

## Stage 4 — Deep Dive: How Serializable Snapshot Isolation Detects Write Skew

- Serializable Snapshot Isolation (SSI), implemented in PostgreSQL since version 9.1, detects write skew by tracking read-write anti-dependencies between concurrent transactions.
- Understanding the internals of this mechanism clarifies why snapshot isolation misses the anomaly and why SSI catches it.
- The Internals: rw-Anti-Dependency Tracking Inside SSI An rw-anti-dependency is formed when one transaction reads a version of a row that another concurrent transaction subsequently writes.
- The reading transaction depended on the "old" version — a version that no longer exists once the writing transaction commits.

*Applies **rate-limiting** to the decision above.*

```mermaid
graph TD
    T1[T1 reads all on_call rows including bob row]
    T2[T2 reads all on_call rows including alice row]
    W1[T1 writes alice row to off_call]
    W2[T2 writes bob row to off_call]

    T1 -->|rw-anti-dep: T1 read bob row that T2 will overwrite| W2
    T2 -->|rw-anti-dep: T2 read alice row that T1 will overwrite| W1
    W1 --> CYCLE[Dangerous cycle - SSI aborts one transaction]
    W2 --> CYCLE
```

**Observable outcome:** The reading transaction depended on the "old" version — a version that no longer exists once the writing transaction commits.

## Stage 5 — From HTTP Request to Empty On-Call Roster: The Full System Architecture View

- Write skew does not only exist in toy examples.
- In a production on-call management system, the anomaly can propagate through multiple layers before causing visible harm.
- The architecture diagram below shows where write skew injects itself into the request flow.
- The write skew injection point is the SVC → DB edge.

*Applies **database-isolation-levels-anomalies** to the decision above.*

```architecture

  "version": 1,
  "title": "From HTTP Request to Empty On-Call Roster: The Full System Architecture View - Subsystem Overview",
  "description": "Decoupled system architecture isolating ingress, stateless logic, and persistent datastores.",
  "view": "high-level",
  "pattern": "microservices",
  "direction": "LR",
  "groups": [
    { "id": "edge", "label": "Edge Traffic Ingress", "tone": "slate" },
    { "id": "services", "label": "Stateless Microservices", "tone": "blue" },
    { "id": "data", "label": "Datastore Infrastructure", "tone": "green" }
  ],
  "nodes": [
    { "id": "gw", "component": "api-gateway", "label": "API Gateway", "group": "edge", "badge": "TLS & Auth" },
    { "id": "app", "component": "workflow-service", "label": "Domain Service", "group": "services", "badge": "Stateless" },
    { "id": "cache", "component": "redis", "label": "Redis Cache", "group": "data", "badge": "Sub-ms Reads" },
    { "id": "db", "component": "postgres", "label": "Transactional DB", "group": "data", "badge": "ACID Log" }
  ],
  "edges": [
    { "from": "gw", "to": "app", "kind": "request", "label": "gRPC Request" },
    { "from": "app", "to": "cache", "kind": "read", "label": "Cache Lookups" },
    { "from": "app", "to": "db", "kind": "write", "label": "Durable Write" }
  ],

  }

```

```mermaid
graph TD
    HTTP1[Alice - HTTP go-off-call request]
    HTTP2[Bob - HTTP go-off-call request]
    SVC[On-Call Availability Service]
    DB[(on_call table - PostgreSQL)]
    SCHED[Emergency Scheduler - polls on-call roster]
    DISP[Emergency Dispatch System]
    ERR[Patient routed with zero on-call doctors]

    HTTP1 --> SVC
    HTTP2 --> SVC
    SVC -->|check + update under Snapshot Isolation| DB
    DB --> SCHED
    SCHED --> DISP
    DISP -->|empty roster query result| ERR
```

**Observable outcome:** The write skew injection point is the SVC → DB edge.

## Stage 6 — Isolation Level Prevention Table: Choosing the Right Defense

- The table below maps each standard isolation level to the anomalies it prevents.
- Read this as a capability matrix — a ✅ means the anomaly is prevented at this level; a ❌ means it can still occur.
- \ PostgreSQL's REPEATABLE READ (implemented as Snapshot Isolation) prevents phantom reads.
- Standard SQL's REPEATABLE READ (as in MySQL InnoDB) does not.

*Applies **caching** to the decision above.*

**Observable outcome:** Standard SQL's REPEATABLE READ (as in MySQL InnoDB) does not.

## End-to-end outcome

After working through the stages, you should be able to explain:

- Repeatable Read is not a safety guarantee for multi-row invariants.
- REPEATABLE READ guarantees that individual rows you have read will not change if you read them again within your transaction.
- Write skew is the anomaly that exposes the gap between "individually correct" and "collectively consistent." The five things to carry away: - Write skew requires two conditions: a shared predicate read by multiple concu…
- If either condition is absent, you have a different anomaly.

## Alternatives considered

The source focuses on one primary design. A second architecture is not compared, so no alternative is invented here.

## Failure and degraded modes

The source does not isolate a separate failure mode. Limits that matter for the scenario are called out in the stage decisions above.

record.markdownContent:
## Scenario context

Fan-out is the act of distributing one post to many followers' feeds. Write-time fan-out (push) pre-computes feeds at post time — fast reads but catastrophic write amplification for celebrities. Read-time fan-out (pull) computes feeds on demand — no amplification but slow reads at scale. Production systems like Twitter/X, Instagram, and Facebook use a **hybrid**: write-time fan-out for users with ≤ 10K followers, re…

This walkthrough focuses on **The Social Feed Problem: One Post, Ten Million Inboxes**.

Before making a design choice, clarify:

- When Justin Bieber tweets, roughly 300 million accounts are eligible to see it.
- Your system has milliseconds to decide: do you immediately push that tweet into every follower's pre-built feed cache, or do you wait and assemble each follower's feed the moment they open the app?
- This is the fan-out problem — the act of distributing a single write event to many downstream consumers — and it is the central architectural decision in every social feed, notification system, and activity stream.

**Concepts in play:** caching, system-design-hld-architectures, database-indexing, event-driven-architecture

## Stage 1 — Deep Dive: Inside the Redis Feed Cache and the Async Fan-Out Pipeline

- The Internals: Redis Sorted Sets, Kafka Topics, and Fan-Out Workers The canonical feed cache data structure is a Redis sorted set ( ZSET ).
- Each follower's feed is stored as a key like feed:{userId} where each member is a postId and the score is the post's Unix timestamp in milliseconds.
- This enables: - ZADD feed:42 1711720800000 postId:9999 — insert a post reference - ZREVRANGE feed:42 0 49 WITHSCORES — fetch the 50 most recent posts - ZREMRANGEBYRANK feed:42 0 -501 — evict entries beyond a 500-post ca…
- Post content is fetched separately in a second read from a post cache or DB, allowing the feed cache to remain compact and fast.

*Applies **caching** to the decision above.*

```
Kafka Topic: post.created
  Partition key: authorId (ensures ordered delivery per author)
  Consumer Group 1: fan-out-workers (writes to Redis feed caches)
  Consumer Group 2: notification-workers (sends push notifications)
  Consumer Group 3: analytics-ingest (feeds the engagement pipeline)
```

**Observable outcome:** Post content is fetched separately in a second read from a post cache or DB, allowing the feed cache to remain compact and fast.

## Stage 2 — The Hybrid Architecture: Routing Posts by Follower Count

- The hybrid model routes the fan-out decision at post time, not at read time.
- The Fan-out Router — consuming from the post.created Kafka topic — checks the author's follower count against a configurable threshold (typically 10,000).
- Normal users fan out immediately; celebrity posts skip the write fan-out entirely and are stored in a dedicated Celebrity Post Store instead.
- The partition key for post.created should be authorId .

*Applies **system-design-hld-architectures** to the decision above.*

```java
@Configuration
public class FanOutKafkaConfig {

    @Bean
    public ConcurrentKafkaListenerContainerFactory<String, PostCreatedEvent> fanOutContainerFactory(
            ConsumerFactory<String, PostCreatedEvent> consumerFactory) {

        ConcurrentKafkaListenerContainerFactory<String, PostCreatedEvent> factory =
            new ConcurrentKafkaListenerContainerFactory<>();

        factory.setConsumerFactory(consumerFactory);
        factory.setConcurrency(8);             // 8 threads per pod, one per Kafka partition
        factory.getContainerProperties()
               .setAckMode(ContainerProperties.AckMode.MANUAL_IMMEDIATE); // Commit only after Redis write succeeds

        return factory;
    }
}

@Component
public class FanOutConsumer {

    @KafkaListener(
        topics = "post.created",
        groupId = "fan-out-workers",
        containerFactory = "fanOutContainerFactory"
    )
    public void consume(PostCreatedEvent event, Acknowledgment ack) {
        fanOutService.handlePostCreated(event);
        ack.acknowledge(); // Only commit offset once fan-out is complete
    }
}
```

**Observable outcome:** The partition key for post.created should be authorId .

## End-to-end outcome

After working through the stages, you should be able to explain:

- Forgetting to handle the celebrity path during cold-start backfill.
- When a user's feed cache expires and is rebuilt from the post DB, it is easy to only restore write-time fan-out posts.
- - Write-time fan-out (push) pre-computes follower feeds at post time using Redis sorted sets.
- Reads are O(1) but writes are O(N followers).

## Alternatives considered

### Fan-Out Fundamentals: The Push vs. Pull Decision

Fan-out refers to the branching factor of a write event: when one user posts, the event must "fan out" to all followers who should see it.

### Write-Time Fan-Out: Paying the Cost at Post Time

When a user with 500 followers posts, a fan-out worker writes 500 entries into Redis — one per follower's sorted set feed cache — with the score set to the post's Unix timestamp.

### Read-Time Fan-Out: Paying the Cost at Read Time

Read-time fan-out inverts the model entirely.


## Failure and degraded modes

The source does not isolate a separate failure mode. Limits that matter for the scenario are called out in the stage decisions above.
